utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. As would be observed, we're getting used to the new technology. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. The OTP this morning, Joanna Korner; starting the most important person in the case, Sebastiaan van Hooydonk, the Case Manager; then Alex Demirdjian; Matthew Olmsted; and I think a new face to Your Honours, but a member of the team for sometime now, Rafael La Cruz; and an intern, Lucy Eastwood sitting in the back.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, Ms. Tatjana Savic and Andreja Zecevic, appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic, Aleksandar Aleksic, Michelle Butler, Miroslav Cuskic, David Martini, Milena Dzudovic, and Ms. Joyce Boekestijn, appearing for Zupljanin Defence team today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So, of course, according to the Scheduling Order, we're here today to begin the closing submissions, and we would invite the OTP to begin.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, before I do that, I sent an e-mail yesterday to the Senior Legal Officer that -- I gather he's not here, but copied to other legal officers in respect of the question of matters of law contained within the Defence final briefs with which we took issue and whether it would be possible to deal with those matters because they're not really the purpose of a final address in writing. Were Your Honours given notification of this application? Your Honour, Mr. Zecevic objects - and I assuming the objection is also maintained on behalf of the Zupljanin team - effectively on the basis that once the final [microphone not activated] ... it has gone off, has it? Oh, yes, I'm told the new microphones are actually less sensitive than the old ones. So, Your Honours, our application this morning is simply this. There are not many but there are some matters of law which we say the Defence have made an error about, and we would simply ask that we can deal with that in writing, and no doubt if Your Honours agree to that OLAD would clearly fund a response from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I'm not sure -- I hear what you have said about the funding issue, but do I understand correctly, and perhaps Mr. Zecevic could confirm this, that the objection is only based on the funding issue and not on any issue of procedural principle? Because the -- as far as the -- the initial view of the Trial Chamber is that this is a matter that is -- can be disposed of in terms of the ordinary principles of how these -- how -- how closings are conducted without venturing into this matter of funding which ordinarily isn't the concern of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you. My -- my objection has nothing to do with the funding. Perhaps that's a misunderstanding by Ms. Korner. My objection was -- was the following: We believed that the Trial Chamber has given ample time for the parties to address all the matters in fact and in law during the closing arguments, and we believe we should do that in the oral arguments. Furthermore, I added that once the closing is done, the Defence team, according to the OLAD policy, does not exist anymore. Therefore, it would be a certain problem for us to -- to -- to deal with the -- with the -- with the written -- written submissions after the closing [microphone not activated] ... of the case. Of course, I assume that this problem can be overcome, but then it will require additional -- additional time for us to discuss that with OLAD and how to do it. And, by the way, a member of Defence teams have been put on notice that after the 1st of June, that they will be no longer needed and people have made some -- some plans to come home -- go home and so on and so forth. But we are in the hands of Your Honours. I mean, it's -- it's not the problem that we cannot overcome. We just believe that it would -- it -- we have enough time, both parties to address these issues during the oral arguments. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, you adopt what Mr. Zecevic has said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It was joint submission by both Defence teams.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, could I hear you further on the procedural aspect. Put aside the funding business.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is -- there are a number of possibilities in respect of final briefs, and one of those possibilities is that there's a response to the final briefs, a written response. Your Honours decided not to -- to afford us the opportunity, which we accept. There are, as Your Honours will hear, we say, many defects in what's asserted in some of the final briefs, but it's the -- the only matter that I'm concerned about is the fact of the law. This is the final oral address. There's an opportunity for both sides to deal with the factual matters that they wish Your Honours to take away with them and also the -- any chance the public gets to hear them. It doesn't seem to us that it's helped by an aery discussion of whether or not [microphone not activated] ... the laws that been probably formulated on certain aspects. I don't think the new and replacement microphones are very effective. So that's the situation, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, we have heard the parties, and we would give this consideration and return with a ruling, probably oral, in the course of today or certainly by tomorrow, first thing tomorrow. Thank you. Yes, Ms. Korner, are you ready to begin?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Yes, it is on. Your Honours, can we start by saying that, as I more or less just said, that the purpose of our closing address today is to highlight some of the matters that we have dealt with at far greater length in the final [microphone not activated] ... trial brief and obviously to deal with some of the matters that have been raised by both accused in their final trial briefs. Can I explain that as has happened through the trial, there will be a division of labour for the purposes of this oral address. Once I have dealt with some preliminary matters, Mr. Demirdjian will deal with the municipalities that Your Honours have heard about in this case. I will then deal with some of the background and the question of resubordination. From there, we move to the liability of Stojan Zupljanin. We are, as it were, building this address in the same way that we built the final trial brief. Mr. Hannis, who is not here at the moment but will be appearing later, will deal with communications, which obviously an important aspect highlighted by both Defence in their briefs, the liability of Mico Stanisic. And Mr. Olmsted will then deal, as he has dealt through most of the trial, with the failure to investigate and to prosecute, which we say applies to both these accused. And, finally, Your Honours, to round off, as it were, all the themes together in one short topic, the -- we will deal with the killings that took place at Koricanske Stijene. Your Honours, can I just say a few general words about the Defence final briefs. In our submission to Your Honours, they invite very careful reading. There are, we would suggest, a number of lacunae in these briefs. For example, propositions with made without any citation. There are assertions of fact about which Your Honours have heard no evidence at all. And, Your Honours, can I take one very simple and straightforward and immediate example of that. It may not be the most important, but it's, we say, unfortunately symptomatic. Your Honours, in the Zupljanin final brief, at paragraph 1, so the very first paragraph. It may not be vital but it's important. It is asserted that Stojan Zupljanin was born on the 22nd of September, 1951, as an only child to a poor, rural family. Well, Your Honours, we checked very carefully and we find no evidence at all that he was an only child to a poor, rural family. As I say, it begins, Your Honour, as it carries on. Your Honour, in paragraph 201, where the brief is dealing with the special police, which I will obviously be returning when I come to deal with Mr. Zupljanin's authority over them, it states: "While they suggested contacting Zupljanin," this is to do with complaints about the behaviour, to address these problems, this was simply because he was known as the head of the CSB, and "he was the most convenient point of contact in the area and the undefined nature of the unit also made it difficult for the Kotor Varos Crisis Staff to know whom to address their complaints." Well, Your Honours, there's not one iota of evidence to that effect. And, Your Honour, finally, if one looks at the Stanisic final brief, at paragraph 53, Your Honours, this goes to the no cites and assertion of facts we say not in evidence: "Some 2.000 MUP employs were dismissed to recruit and employ Muslim policemen on the pretext that it was necessary to achieve ethnic balance between the service." There is absolutely no cite for that proposition. The next part for which there is a cite is to Mr. Andan, and that doesn't in any way deal with that assertion there at the beginning of paragraph 53. Your Honours, further, we say that there are really misleading assertions, regrettably, in the brief. Your Honours, sticking with the Stanisic brief for the moment, paragraph 99, Your Honour, this comes under the section which is headed the previous page: No plan to split the MUP. And they say at the end of the paragraph, having -- the document that they're dealing with is, in fact, 1D116. And it says: "The document highlights the major problem created by the SDA leadership by pushing the MUP into a conflict with the JNA. This was done, in part, by the take-over of military records for the creating of an armed force to confront the army." Your Honours, I'm going to ask that we put up 1D116, please. Or part of it. This was a public announcement. If Your Honours look, this was the -- the BiH MUP making a public announcement about the statement made by Dr. Karadzic. And at the end, they list their complaints, we see -- it's the penultimate paragraph with a dash: "- creating an anti-army atmosphere, which is apparent in the MUP written order to engage the police in preventing the JNA ... from taking over military records... " So what was happening there was they were preventing the JNA, not taking over the military reports [microphone not activated] ... so, Your Honours, the reason we're giving a few examples at this stage is simply so that when reading these briefs, Your Honours do check the various cites. Can I take one example of this from the Zupljanin final brief; paragraph 235. This, Your Honour, is a part of the -- I can only call it a diatribe, I'll come back to that, that -- that the Zupljanin final brief engages in against Mr. Brown, the military expert. And they say there that: "Prosecution expert, Brown, was forced to concede that an order issued by General Talic provided that police in exceptional circumstances may be used in a variety of different ways to support the army and that importantly they may be used for combat activities without forming MUP organs or obtaining their approval." And the cite there is for Mr. Brown's evidence. And pursuant to Talic's order discretion to resubordinate police in such circumstances was vested in the army. Such exceptional circumstances, i.e., war, were in fact the norm through the indictment period. Now, the suggestion that is made is that what is what Mr. Brown said. In fact, that was not what Mr. Brown said. Mr. Brown gave an example of exceptional circumstances. I just -- for a moment -- the passage. Sorry about that. Which is not cited. It's -- it begins at the bottom of T18916. And he said about the exceptional circumstances: "I would read this as bearing in mind the context of the time and this comes in the middle of the corridor operation but this is relating to the front line. I have maybe mentioned this in direct. Front line combat tasks, for example, that were occurring in the corps in that time in the corridor," and that in exceptional circumstances, presumably he means here, if there is a weakness in the front line or there is a counter-attack by the enemy formation that "in exceptional circumstances, police can be used but there are limitations and that they are to hold and strengthen the front prior to the arrival of military units." So in essence, it is to plug a front line if there's a problem. And he goes on to say at page 18949: "So I read this document in the context of what was happening in the corridor." He did not say that exceptional circumstances were war. And, of course, the Defence use that to show that war means that all stages, the army could resubordinate the police. And, Your Honour, I will, as I say, come back to that. Your Honours, there are sentences taken out of context. Judge Harhoff was quoted with approval at paragraph 420. May wish to read what he said before and after the page that is quoted. And, finally, Your Honours, what we would call false syllogisms. Your Honours, it is particularly noted in paragraph 282 of the Zupljanin brief. And I'm sure Your Honours are aware of what a syllogism is. I'm having difficulty in saying it myself. Your Honours, at paragraph 282, and we're still dealing with resubordination, the Defence assert that -- this is following on from the Law on Internal Affairs, the Geneva Conventions, that: "Any involvement by civilian police in arresting, detaining, interrogating suspects during an armed conflict occurred outside the legal parameters of normal police duties. These are military tasks. It follows that the only situation in which the police could be ordered to engage in such tasks would be if they were resubordinated to the army." Once this happened, military rules and laws applied to the individual police officers involved. In other words, and what we say is the false syllogism is, the police are not allowed to guard prisoners by law, the military are, ergo, if the police were guarding therefore they must be resubordinated. And there's -- I'm sure Your Honours can see there's a definite missing link there because the obvious answer is, well, by law they may not have been allowed to do it. This doesn't mean they didn't. It does not automatically follow that they were resubordinated. Your Honours, two other matters before I invite Mr. Demirdjian to tell Your Honours about what we say about municipalities. The Defence, not surprisingly, rely very heavily on the witnesses who were former senior members of the MUP and who came to testify largely for the Prosecution. As we said in our final brief, it's for Your Honours, of course, to assess the weight and the truthfulness of that evidence. But, of course, most of them, if not all, had been interviewed by the Office of the Prosecutor as suspects. Many of them were clearly a party to what we say was the joint criminal enterprise, and all of them had their own interests to serve. And it's for Your Honours to assess, as we say, how much weight you give their evidence. The second matter is this: In one sense, the Defence have had the advantage of being able to blame dead men; in particular, Mr. Drljaca and Todorovic, and the advantage that in the dock, in the -- with both these accused has been nobody who represented either the military or the political side. And the third thing, Your Honours, is this: In the Defence pre-trial briefs, both the original and the supplementary ones which were ordered, there is not a hint, Your Honour, of one of the major Defences that has been run in this case. The fact that both accused who are going to be saying as a major plank of their case that neither of them had authority over the members of the RS MUP who committed crimes as anything between 80 and 100 per cent, and I'll come to those calculations later, were resubordinated at the time of the crimes being committed, whether they were in take-overs or guarding camps. The nearest that one comes in any of the pre-trial briefs was paragraph 17 of the Zupljanin final -- pre-trial brief where he stated that the role of the police was minor in comparison with the role of the army and that his -- Zupljanin's de jure position did not correspond with his de facto power. And Your Honours are entitled to ask why such a major plank of the Defence was never mentioned in either pre-trial brief. Your Honours, finally, can I turn to the municipalities. Your Honours, we are going to address in the beginning the events there for the following reasons: The crimes for which the accused, we say, are criminally liable happened there; the evidence shows a pattern which leads to the irresistible inference that these crimes happened by design, or these events happened by design, not chance, but they are both widespread and systematic. And because the only mention of the victims, really, in this case has come through the Defence attempts to challenge the evidence that named victims either died as a result of the crimes, or challenging their civilian status by saying, by seeking to say, that at some time or other those victims had been members of the opposing forces. And Your Honours know, we say without any proper justification for so saying. The victims for these crimes were the reason for the establishment of this Court. As one sees on the poster coming into the lobby of this building, "Bringing war criminals to justice and justice to victims." The nature of trials of high-level accused means that unlike the earlier trials at this court, their voices, the voices of the victims, have not been heard. And the most that, really, Your Honours heard from victims of these crimes was from those who came to deal with disputed or disallowed adjudicated facts, and regrettably because of the time limitations and those limitations, in fact, were quite often not able to explain to the Court, when they tried to, about what personally happened to them. And so we start, we hope, properly by reminding the Court of the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. As announced by Ms. Korner, I will be dealing with the pattern of the evidence that emerged out of the municipalities in this case. Before I deal with the specifics, it is useful to remind ourselves of some of the context in which the pattern developed. Now, Your Honours, as Bosnia and Herzegovina declared its independence and with the likelihood of international recognition, the Bosnian Serb leadership opposed an independent Bosnia and decided to create a separate Serb state on large parts of Bosnia's territory. To achieve this, the Serb leadership created a parallel government and forcibly removed hundreds of thousands of Muslims and Croats in what turned out to be a well-developed deliberate plan. The crimes that came about as a result of this plan follow a clear pattern showing that the crimes charged in the indictment were not committed in isolation but, rather, were guided by a common theme. Looking at the pattern inevitably means looking at the evidence of victims who came to The Hague to recount what must have been the worst experiences of their lives. We will look at what they said in court and what contemporaneous documents tell us about the emergence of this pattern. The first aspect I would like to deal with is the arming of Serbs prior to the beginning of the conflict. Your Honours, there is no dispute that Muslims and Croats sought the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that Bosnian Serbs opposed it. However, the accused have alleged in their Defence that all sides were arming themselves as ethnic groups became suspicious of one another. They have also alleged that the Bosnian Serb leadership's actions were merely reactive or defensive. They claim they did not share the intent of forcibly removing Muslims and Croats and that what occurred in 1992 was a by-product of the conflict. As Your Honours will have seen from our final brief, the evidence tells a different story. The Prosecution does not claim that Muslims and Croats were not arming themselves. However, it is submitted that the Bosnian Serbs prepared themselves, not to the defend against Muslim or Croat physical aggression, but rather to implement their objectives by forced after the loss of their political battle in blocking the recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a sovereign state. Several speeches made during Serb Assembly sessions prior to the conflict make it clear that the Bosnian Serb leadership had in mind to concur by force large portions of Bosnia's territory. Momcilo Krajisnik said very clearly during the 8th session when he stated the following: "Gentlemen, we want to remain in a single state together with Serbia, Montenegro, the Independent Autonomous Region of Krajina, now the Krajina state, and the rest. We just need to agree on the method to achieve this. If we don't want this to be by certain methods, let us put a stop to it. You know what our profession has always been - to wage war." It is against this background that the Bosnian Serb armed themselves. During the pre-conflict period, the Bosnia Serb leadership requested the assistance of the JNA. Indeed, during the session of the December 11th, 1991, Krajisnik highlighted the necessity to address a demand to the JNA stressing its obligation to protect the territories, and I quote, "We have proclaimed an integral part of the federal state." By this time, Your Honour, the republics were virtually left without any weapons as military weapons and equipment from the TO warehouses had already been removed by the JNA by the end of 1990. What followed was a systematic distribution of weapons throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina by the JNA. Weapons were distributed to local SDS committees in Bosnian Serb claimed territories. This was a well orchestrated operation and involved the use of trucks and helicopters. For example, in Prijedor, many members of the 5th Kozarac Brigade returned from the Croatia battle-front and kept their weapons at home. Shipments of weapons were delivered by trucks and helicopters during spring of 1992 and the Serb villages of Balte, Petrov Gaj, and Cirkin Polje. The Serb staff members of the SJB used the premises of the social centre in Cirkin Polje to store weapons. In his end-of-year report, Simo Drljaca reported that: "The focus of the work was on the covert organisation and formation of shadow police stations and the arming and equipping of the personnel. In this manner, 13 police stations were established with a total of about 1500. Weapons, ammunition and other materiel were acquired from various sources - the army was the primary source - and secretly, mostly at night, collected, transported, stored, and distributed to personnel for home keeping and use." This is in Exhibit P689. In Doboj, JNA barracks were located at the outskirts of town with a military presence of the 6th Motorised Brigade manned by about a thousand soldiers by the beginning of conflict and several other units including a JNA artillery unit. Starting in October 1991, five or six volunteer detachments had been created by the JNA each being manned 3- to 400 persons. They received their weapons from the JNA, and Your Honours have seen the receipts for such distribution at Exhibit P2446. Finally, in Zvornik, the SJB reported in its end-of-year report that: "Working on various check-points during the months of January and February, police personnel of Serb nationality enabled the transport of weapons, ammunition and other materiel and technical equipment necessary for the arming of the Serb people in the territory of this municipality." These are but a few examples, Your Honours, of how the Bosnian Serb leadership systematically organised the arming of the Serbs in towns and villages and municipalities claimed to be an integral part of Serb territory. I will now move on to the take-overs. By the end of 1991, Your Honour, the Serb leadership had already created an assembly. They had indicated which municipalities fell under the territory they claim to be Serb. If you will remember after the plebescite, they issued a decision confirming the territory of each SAO. They proclaim on the 9th of the January, 1992, the republic of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. In the following weeks they adopted a constitute and the laws necessary to govern the republic. All they needed was a green light to assume power over the claimed territories. That green light came on the 24th of March, the same day that Mr. Stanisic was appointed minister of the interior. During the 12th Assembly, Radovan Karadzic convinced the Assembly that they did not need a national guard like the one that was created in Croatia. Indeed, Karadzic was happy with having the JNA on his side, and he added that a national guard was not necessary as "numbers in the police are quite sufficient." He followed by uttering these prophetic words. First he said: "We have a legal basis in the Law on Internal Affairs. "We also have the insignia. "At a desired moment, and this will be very soon, we can form whatever we want. "This could happen in two of three days." And: "At that moment, all the Serbian municipalities, both the old ones and the newly established ones, would literally assume control on the entire territory of the municipality concerned." Karadzic continues by stating that in Zvornik control would be assumed over everything that constitutes the Serbian municipality of Zvornik. He continued by saying this: "Then, at a given moment, in the next three or four days, there will be a single method used and you will be able to apply it in the municipalities you represent, including both things that must be done as well as how to do them. How to separate the police ... take the resources that belong to the Serbian people, and take command." Your Honours, it is no coincidence that Zvornik was forcibly taken over within weeks of this speech and it was one of the first municipalities to be taken over. Now take-overs seem to have followed a similar pattern depending on the level of control exerted by the Bosnian Serbs in each municipality. For example, in Pale and Bileca which were Serb majority municipalities, Bosnian Serbs assumed power over municipal organs such as the police, the Assembly and their institutions several weeks before attacks took place on surrounding villages; whereas in other municipalities, such as Sanski Most, Doboj or Bosanski Samac the take-over was marked by an attack, an armed attack, against vital institutions. The take-overs were conducted simultaneously over the course of three months. Now, this animated slide will show you how these municipalities were taken over. The municipalities in the indictment on this map will be coloured in red in a moment. Those that are not in the indictment will be coloured in grey. The municipalities that are not in the indictment for which we do have a take-over date will also be part of the chronology, whereas the rest will be highlighted at the end. Now, in the first animation you can see that by the end of the March, Pale, Ilijas and Bijeljina had already been taken over. By the end of the first week of April, you could see that Banja Luka and Teslic have been taken over. By the end of the second week in April, Zvornik and Visegrad were taken over. By the end the third week of April, Donji Vakuf, Bosanski Samac, and Vlasenica were also taken over. By the end of the fourth week in April, Prijedor and Sanski Most fell as well. Hence by the end of April 1992, 12 of the 19 charged municipalities were under Serb control. Now, by the end the first week of May, Brcko, Doboj, Skender Vakuf and Kljuc were taken over. Following this, by the end of May, pretty much every municipality in the ARK had been taken over, except for Kotor Varos. In the first week of June, Gacko was taken over. And this was followed by Bileca and Kotor Varos which were both taken over by the middle of June. By the end of June, Modrica was taken over and this marked the opening of the Posavina corridor. During the first week of July, Derventa is taken over, enlarging the corridor. And we will see that in October, Bosanski Brod was also taken over. By the end the year, all of the municipalities highlighted on this map were effectively under Serb control. Your Honours, may have already found that the take-overs have not been mentioned once in the Stanisic Defence final brief, while Zupljanin claims in his brief that the take-overs were conducted by the army and that the involvement of the police, if any, was in a resubordinated capacity. The evidence shows, Your Honours that in some cases, yes, the army did -- took part and led forcible take-overs, whereas in other cases the army played no role whatsoever and is seen later taking part in joint attacks. We will start with Bijeljina which was, as you have seen already, taken over on the 31st of March, and was the result of a combined attack involving the Serb TO, Mauzer's national guard, Arkan's volunteer guard with the support of the JNA. That day, the police had the role of protect the vital facilities in town. Following the take-over the SJB chief reported the following: "I have managed to procure some of the equipment, berets and badges with the tricolour from the Serbian MUP and our police officers have worn them since the [sic] first day when they went out on the streets on the 4th of April, 1992." Stories of civilians being arrested and mistreated in Bijeljina quickly circulated at the time and spread throughout the country. In the first days of the attack, 48 bodies had been picked up prior to Biljana Plavsic's visit on the 4th of April. In Zvornik, Your Honours, the take-over took place on the 8th of April, and by this time the police had already split and the Serb police force had established its headquarters in the Alhos factory where the Crisis Staff and Arkan's Men were also stationed. Following an ultimatum issued by the Serb forces, the police, the TO, the JNA, and Arkan's men launched their attack on Zvornik town. The attack on Zvornik was of great violence as is best summarised by the UN envoy in the following clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: "That day an UN official was driving from Serbia to Bosnia. He was stopped just outside Zvornik. "[No interpretation] Everybody is crazy." "A paramilitary commander proud of his work let in a news crew. Here, the regime of terror is being established as military police try to identify the Muslims." "[No interpretation]"

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, about a week after Zvornik, Bosanski Samac fell. The town was taken over with the careful planning both by the police, the JNA and the TO. All Serb police officers deserted the police station and left one Bosnian Croat policeman on duty, Luka Gregurevic. On the night of the 16th of April, Samac was a deserted town. The restaurants were empty and one could feel that something was about to happen. On 17th April around 2.00 in the morning gun-shots a loud explosion were heard in town. Bosanski Samac was taken over by the Serb police and the Serb TO by securing government institutions, as this was reported in a report of the 17th Corps headquarters as you can see on the screen at this moment. The police station was attacked and taken over and the new chief, Stevan Todorovic, assumed his position that day. Three weeks later, Luka Gregurevic, who was on duty, would be executed in Crkvine. On the same day, the 17th of April, the police station in Sanski Most was split among ethnic lines, and the police chief, Dragan Majkic, distributed the new RS berets and had his staff sign the loyalty oath. Two days later, the SDS president, Nedeljko Rasula, issued an ultimatum to the SDA to vacate the municipal building otherwise the building would come under attack. The building was indeed vacated however a few non-Serb policemen remained inside. At 10.00 in the morning, on the 19th of April, the Serb Defence forces, the SOS attacked the municipal building and took it over. The next day, CSB Banja Luka and the Serbian news agency --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Demirdjian, I don't know if you have see the court reporter's note.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, I will slow down, Your Honours. Thank you. The next day on the 20th of April, CSB Banja Luka and the Serbian news agency in Sarajevo were informed of this take-over by letter. On 19th of April, Vlasenica's Serb Crisis Staff issued an unambiguous order entitled: "Decision to take power." On that day, all non-Serb policemen were disarmed. And the next day on the 20th of April, units of the JNA's Novi Sad corps and the Serbian Guard unit from Sekovici took control of all municipal institutions in Vlasenica. In Prijedor, the accused Zupljanin claims that the army and the Crisis Staff led the take-over. In fact, take-over was organised by the Serb police and the military. Once again, the SJB chief was very candid in his end-of-year report. Looking back of the achievements of his station in 1992, he wrote the following: "As a result in the night between 29 and 30 April ... following very detailed preparations and pursuant to the relevant decisions of the executive committee of the Serbian municipality of Prijedor, an organised take-over of power was embarked upon. About 400 policemen assembled in the social centre at Cirkin Polje, and at 4.00 in the morning they took control of all important sites in town, which immediately made possible the take-over of all leading functions in the municipality, the municipal organs and the important companies." During the month of May, Brcko was the first municipality to be taken over, on the 1st to be exact. It was followed by Doboj which was taken over during the night of the 2nd to the 3rd of May. The attack on Doboj was orchestrated by the JNA and involved volunteer detachments led by Major Stankovic, units of the 6th Motorised Brigade, Red Berets from Serbia led by Radojica Bozovic, and the civilian police. CSB Doboj officials had been meeting with Serb army officials for weeks prior to the take-over. The CSB chief himself was on Mount Ozren the night of the take-over at the moment when the take-over operation began. Your Honours have heard allegations that the take-over was ordered by Mr. Cazim Hadzic, the 6th Motorised Brigade's commander. However, you have heard evidence that he was arrested the night of the take-over and was in fact sidelined for months prior to the take-over. This allegation is not credible. In relation to the CSB building, Your Honour, the scenario was similar to the one in Bosanski Samac. Virtually all Serb police officers had deserted the police building and a non-Serb policeman was left in charge of the duty service. A little after midnight, armed men entered this police building and arrested non-Serb employees and beat them up. The police entered the station the next morning and the Serb forces helped taking over a number of other buildings in town. As of that day, Your Honours, all non-Serb police officers were dismissed and at least one Muslim inspector was directly informed of his dismissal by the CSB chief, Bjelosevic. The last take-over which is charged in the indictment was in Kotor Varos, Zupljanin's birth place, and it was raided by the special police detachment on the 11th of June, 1992, at dawn. This Trial Chamber has had the rare opportunity to view a video of this take-over and we will now look at some excerpts. Now the first excerpt we will see in the morning hours of the 11th of June - and we can play it now - is a special unit entering the SJB building.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You can see the entrance of the police station right there. And you will see in a moment a number of members of the special police detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now in the second excerpt, we see the special police leaving the SJB building and you will notice here Ljuban Bajic [sic] wearing a red beret. He is one of the leaders of the special unit. Bajic. Ljuban Ecim, my apologies. We now see one of the blue tanks used by the CSB Banja Luka. Similar tanks were seen on the 12th of May parade. And in a moment we will also see the first non-Serbs arrested that morning. Here a member of the special unit orders a man to stand against the wall and show a three-finger sign. The third excerpt we will see is a special police forcing a civilian to open the trunk of his car with some brutality.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: In the fourth excerpt, we see the special police asking a civilian peacefully walking in the street to lay down, and he kicks him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: In the fifth excerpt we now see the special police surrounding a house. As Your Honours will see in a moment, the special police were allegedly searching for dangerous Muslim and Croat extremists. Those are extremists that the Bosnian Serb leadership was concerned about. In bright daylight, under no attacks, the special police easily arrested Muslim and Croat civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: These are the dangerous extremists, Your Honours. And the last excerpt we will see, on that day, the Serb flag was hoisted on the municipal police station, the SJB.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, some municipalities were taken over by relatively non-violent means, as the Serb civilian and military leadership were already in a position to control the municipality. We can see the next map, Your Honours will remember hearing evidence that in municipalities of Kljuc, Pale, Bileca and Teslic, non-Serb policemen were convened to meetings by their respective SJB leaders and were simply told they could no longer work in the police. Attacks on Muslim and Croats villages followed many weeks later at a time where Serb control had already been imposed on the municipality. This pattern equally applied to municipalities not charged in the indictment. For example, you have heard evidence that in Bratunac, all Muslims were fired from their work in mid-April 1992 and all the key positions and the local government were taken over by the Serb authorities.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: What emerges from the evidence, Your Honours, is a pattern of forcible take-overs throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina with a varying degree of violence depending on level of control exerted by Serb authorities prior to the take-over. I will now move on to the issue of persecutory measures imposed following the take-over. The take-over of municipalities marked, Your Honours, the beginning of a period of excessive measures applied against Muslims and Croats, including large-scale arrested, unlawful detention, torture and cruel treatment during periods of detention, killings, and other persecutory acts such as limitation of movement and the forcible transfer and deportation of civilians. Your Honour, may remember the evidence of Sulejman Tihic, president of the SDA in Bosanski Samac. A lawyer by profession, like most of us in this room, he had his law office in Bosanski Samac. However, a few days after the take-over he was arrested and suffered some of the most depraved forms of mistreatment. To add to the injury he was publicly humiliated by being forced to sweep the streets outside the police station of the municipal building while being watched by all passers-by. In most municipalities, Your Honours, prominent Muslims and Croats were dismissed from their managerial positions and this includes judges, police station commanders, company managers, et cetera. Setting aside managers, even employees were told they could not come to work. In Banja Luka, already in late 1991, non-Serb directors and managers as well as factory employers were dismissed. And in schools teaches were already forced to use the Cyrillic script. Much later on the 18th of June, 1992, all non-Serb employees from the hospital were dismissed. We can move to the next slide. You have heard similar dismissals in Sanski Most where Judge Adil Draganovic refused to sign a loyalty oath to the new authorities, and he was fired from his position as a judge. He also lost all his property and his house which were torched while he was in detention. In Doboj, you heard Edin Hadzovic who told you that he worked for the association of physical education organisations. He was a cashier. Hadzovic was told by Jovo Popovic, a manager of this enterprise, that he and other non-Serb employees had to leave as Popovic was told to dismiss all non-Serbs. This was shortly prior to the take-over. In the next slides, you will see Sulejman Crncalo. You have heard his evidence. You've -- he's told you how he was dismissed. On the 15th of May he arrived at work at the Famos factory where he had worked since 1978 and where he held the position of chief of the development department. That day, he was told by the guard at the gate that he could not enter. Some employees were allowed in but no Muslims were allowed. Now Your Honours have already heard examples of curfews in various municipalities. I will simply mention that in the municipalities of Kljuc, in Doboj, in Teslic, in Gacko, in Kotor Varos, and even in Zvornik you have evidence of this curfew being announced and imposed unequally and solely against non-Serbs. I'll now move on to the large-scale arrests that occurred following the take-overs. Your Honours, from one municipality to the other, Muslims and Croats were arrested and taken to local police stations where they were detained for varying periods of time. Usually arrests started in town and focussed on prominent Muslims and Croats. The aim was clear: By neutralising the leadership of the non-Serb communities, the non-Serb population was paralysed and posed no threat to Serb ambitions. In Pale, again you heard from Mr. Crncalo that a number of Muslims were arrested randomly in the streets by the civilian police and were taken to the SJB building and were held there. In Banja Luka, you have heard of policemen in blue camouflage uniform driving around in a red van, which was also called the "red kombi," arresting non-Serbs in the streets and beating them in the van. The doors were always left open to this van so other residents could hear the beatings and the screams. This method was used to intimidate other Muslims and Croats in the neighbourhood. These were members of public and state security in Banja Luka considered to be heros by Stojan Zupljanin. In Zvornik, you heard how on the 1st of June, hundreds of Muslim civilians from the villages of Setici and Klisa were chased out of their village by the army who had surrounded it with tanks. The villagers were forced to walk to the village of Djulici where 750 men were separated from the convoy by police officers and were taken to a Karakaj technical school. In Brcko, non-Serbs were arrested throughout town and taken to various camps. For example, on the 4th of May, Jasmin Fazlovic, who worked in the fire station, was arrested with four other non-Serbs by Captain Dragan and Mirko Blagojevic. They were taken to the SJB. There, they were received by the SJB chief, Dragan Veselic, who accused them of being Green Berets and sent them to the Luka camp where he said, You will be killed. You also heard from Isak Gasi, a former athlete who was quite well-known in Yugoslavia. He was arrested by two preliminary, Dragan Pantelic and Stevo Knezevic who took him without being told the reasons for his arrest and were -- and he was taken to the SJB building. After being detained there for an hour, he was taken to the Luka camp which was situated 3- to 400 metres away from the police station. It is worth noting that the Stanisic Defence brief claims that the Luka camp was near Brcko. However, the evidence is clear, that the camp was in Brcko. When Gasi arrived there, about 200 non-Serbs were held there. You also heard evidence of a similar pattern in Vogosca where about 470 men, women and children were arrested following the take-over of the villages of Svrake and Semizovac in early 1992. If we can look at the next slide, in Bosanski Samac, mass arrested started immediately with the take-over and were carried out throughout spring and summer of 1992. On the 15th of May, the Serb municipality issued the following unequivocal decision: "All people of Croatian nationality on the territory of the Serbian municipality of Bosanski Samac shall be isolated and deployed to vital facilities in the town and in villages." The SJB chief, Todorovic, gave evidence that Croats were actually detained in such vital facilities as they knew that these were likely to be targeted by the Croatian army. Your Honour, one of the pervasive aspects of the pattern that we observed in this case was the establishment of detention facilities where civilians were held in inhumane conditions and where brutality varied only in degree. The existence of such facility in every municipality charged in the indictment is sufficient by itself to demonstrate a pattern too uniform to be ad hoc; instead, one that must be a product of a guiding hand above the municipality level. That inescapable conclusion is only bolstered by fact that camps were set up and run by the army, the police, the Crisis Staffs, all with their chain of command up to the Presidency, the government, and, more particularly to Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin. The detention of civilians was systemic. Officials at all levels knew about the camps and the republican exchange commission was established from the earlier stage to monitor and control the possible release of civilians. Now, as described at paragraph 650 and 651 in our final brief, non-Serbs were detained in makeshift detention facilities from the outbreak of the conflict, and both Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin were aware of the existence of such facilities. In Pale where Stanisic had his headquarters at the beginning of the conflict, Muslims and Croats were detained in an old culture centre next to the police station. Other detention centres included the movie theatre and military barracks in Hrenovica. Kemal Hujdur described how, following the attack on Hrenovica in mid-May, around 25 Muslims were taken to the SJB and were beaten in front of the station. The detainees were then brought to the old cultural centre where about 20 non-Serbs were already imprisoned. Beating continues there. Looking at this next map, Your Honours, you will find the 52 detention centres charged in the indictment. Of course, more camps existed in other municipalities not charged in the indictment, such as in Rogatica, Ilidza, Sokolac and Ugljevik. They will not appear on this [indiscernible]. Your Honours can see that detention centres were established in every one of the five regions within the RS. Of the 52, there are 48 which were established by the RS MUP. Only two were under the jurisdiction of the minister -- Ministry of Justice; that is, the Doboj Central Prison and Planjo's house which is an annex to the Kula prison. Two other detention camps were established by the army; namely, Manjaca and Batkovic. All other camps charged in the indictment were operated and manned by members of the civilian police under Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin. Before I get to the conditions in these camps, is this an appropriate time to take a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. It appears so, Mr. Demirdjian. So we would return in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian, before you continue, I would remind you to pace yourself so that -- because it is a natural tendency that we all have to speed up particularly when we deal with written --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I have been reminded by the interpreters as well. Thank you, Your Honours. Before the break, Your Honours, we were reaching the stage where we were discussing the conditions in the detention camps. Now we have heard repeatedly from victims detained in these facilities that the conditions were simply appalling. Conditions for proper hygiene did not exist. You heard from ST-08 from Teslic who was held in the SJB cells. He recognised several prominent members of the Muslim community in Teslic, and there were up to 50 Muslims and Croats held in the cells at one point, clearly inadequate for the number of detainees held there. What he said was this: "At some point we couldn't sit. We had to stand up. People used to stand up even in the toilet. You could smell the ammonia from the urine, so it was quite unbearable. The tears used to come out of our eyes because of the smell of the ammonia. We used to shout, Give us some air or kill us, because we needed some air." Beatings were commonplace at the SJB building in -- several times non-Serbs would be beaten at the entrance of the SJB and detainees in the cells could hear and watch the beating. At least on one occasion the police chief, Dusan Kuzmanovic, and the police commander, Predrag Markocevic, watched the beatings from the entrance of the station, standing there laughing. Such beatings in the SJB building and later at the TO warehouse would lead to the death of several non-Serb civilians. In Donji Vakuf, the police was involved with the army in attacking villages inhabited by Muslims. Following such attacks, the police reported that there was a need to establish an collection centre for Croatians and Muslim men. And the SJB dealt with everything and the police were in charge of providing security. This was reported by the SJB chief himself. The SJB reported that during the month of June it was holding 123 Muslims and Croats and that it had transferred 28 detainees to Manjaca camp. But it is in Prijedor, it is the camps in Prijedor, which became the epitome of dreadful conditions in detention facilities. The camps of Keraterm, Omarska, and Trnopolje captured the attention of the international media in July of 1992 and clearly sent a signal to the Serb authorities that what was happening in these places were clearly unacceptable. Lack of access to proper hygiene, lack of food, and daily beatings were part of the diet imposed on the prisoners held in Prijedor camps. The authorities in Prijedor did not label Omarska or Trnopolje as camps, as you will see in the following video. During the visit of the international media, the prisoners were too scared to describe the conditions at these camps. The video begins at the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: "Here, we were shown only several hundred of the two and a half thousand prisoners or Muslim men at Omarska we were told to be interrogated. Those fund guilty of fighting Serbs were then sent to prisoner of war camps, the innocents to refugee camps "This is all we saw of the prisoners and of Omarska itself. "They never spoke. "The only voice those of the guards ordering them to eat faster and leave. "How are you treated? What are the conditions, I asked. "I don't want to tell lies. I can't speak the truth. Thank you for coming. "We were told that the army does not control Omarska. These prisoners are the responsibility of the civil authorities and local malitia. We sought an explanation from the camp commandant."

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: We can pause here. You can see here at the left the SJB chief, Simo Drljaca, and to the right Nada Balaban, the administrator of the Omarska camp. Can you continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: "[Indiscernible] This is a prison camp, a transit camp or a refugee camp. "No, this is not the camp, this is the centre, the transit centre. Omarska and Trnopolje, both the centres, not camps. "And then the men left, back to wherever they'd come from, away from our cameras and questions, hidden from United Nations and the Red Cross who have been denied access to Omarska, hidden until now from the world. We were not allowed to follow them to the living accommodation what appeared to be the larger of the two buildings, to see the other 2.000 detainees and how they lived. "What's your reason? "[Indiscernible] to do my best here. "Show us where they live "Why are you not fulfilling Dr. Karadzic's promise to us? "He promised us something else and said you can do this and this and that and not that. "We see nothing. We see one dining hall and 80 persons. "So we left. Our host fulfilling their promise to show us the second camp, Trnopolje, where 2.000 refugees are living. We were not prepared for what we saw and heard there."

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: The visit of the international media left the world with an unforgettable image of a terrified doctor, Idriz Merdzanic, as he is being asked by the journalist about the conditions in Trnopolje camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: "We, ourselves, saw no evidence of beatings on any refugee here and we only heard the allegations, allegations even the camp doctor seemed unable to substantiate in front of our Serb hosts. "[Indiscernible] cases here of people who have been beaten from the other camps? "[No interpretation] yes. "Many? "[No interpretation] "Would you be happy speaking in another language? "Yes. "I was able, however, to smuggle out a role of film and the man who took these pictures and gave it to me said he would be called if caught. He begged me to check that in three days he was still alive."

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: This is the detention facility which was labelled as a transit centre, Your Honours. With the limited time we have, it would be impossible to expose the details of every single detention facility, suffice it to say that in most of these facilities one can observe striking similarities: In all cases, detainees are Muslim or Croat civilians. Detainees are never informed of the reasons behind their arrest. The detainees are underfed and lose a considerable amount of weight. The detainees are repeatedly beaten and mistreated by guards, soldiers, policemen, and members of paramilitary units. Several detainees die of their injuries. In some facilities, such as the sawmill in Kotor Varos, detained women are raped repeatedly by guards and soldiers or policemen who entered the facility. Some women became pregnant as a result. In some cases, detainees are executed in large numbers while being detained. The following incidents spring to mind: Massacre of about 180 Muslim and Croat civilians in room 3 at Keraterm camp. The murder of 80 Muslim and Croat men in the Crkvina warehouse in Bosanski Samac. The murder of dozens of non-Serbs held at Luka camp, Brcko. Murder of about 175 men at Gero's slaughter-house and the killing of about 20 non-Serbs at the Celopek Dom Kultur at Zvornik, as well as the killing non-Serb civilians held at the Susica camp in Vlasenica in the summer of 1992. Your Honours, another mean to -- another means to ensure the spread of terror with the aim of forcing the non-Serb population to leave Serb-held territory came through the acts of murder whereby dozens of Muslims and Croat civilians were coldly executed. You have heard evidence of killings at Velagici in the municipality of Kljuc where 77 Muslim men were killed after being detained shortly in the school. They were collected from surrounding villages from their homes. In Brcko, town of Brcko, became a large killing site during 1992. Non-Serbs who were detained in the camp in the SJB in the Partizan hall, the Laser bus company were routinely subjected to tortures and killings. You heard from Isak Gasi that he witnessed the killing of civilians in one of the streets leading to the market place on the 6th or the 7th of May. Mr. Gasi was in a building in the old part of town when he saw at a distance of about 30 to 40 metres a policeman dressed in a typical civilian police uniform. The policeman shot and killed three civilians right there in the street. About 50 metres away he saw men in camouflage uniforms killing about 12 more civilians. In a now famous series of photographs captured in Brcko at the time, Gasi was able to identify the same street where these killings occurred. You will see on the first slide a policeman, on the second slide a policeman aiming at a civilian, and the third picture a civilian lying down. Bodies were picked up by a refrigerator truck which was frequently seen coming and going in the streets of Brcko. This picture shows how these bodies were discarded in a mass grave in Brcko. In Visegrad on the 14th of June a group of non-Serb civilians from the village of Koritnik, mainly women, children, and the elderly were forced to flee their village. Arriving in Visegrad on foot, the group was placed in houses on Pionirska Street in the Muslim neighbourhood of Mahala which is located 400 metres away from the police station. Soon thereafter, Milan and Sredoje Lukic, along with other armed Serbs arrived at the house. They first robbed the villagers of their valuables, before leaving, taking one woman with them whom they would later rape. Later that night the Lukic brothers [sic] and other armed Serbs moved this group to a house next door. They locked them up in a single room. The house was set on fire. Those detained who tried to escape through the windows were shot. Approximately 60 people were burned alive in this house fire. This next map, Your Honours, will illustrate the killings charged in the indictment. And I will summarise. For the month of May in the first wave - we'll go to the first animation - we can see killings in various locations, such as the prison in Vlasenica; the killing of 22 non-Serbs at Nova Kasaba taken from the Vlasenica prison; the Drinjaca school in Zvornik; the killing of over 800 non-Serb civilians during the attack and shelling of the village of Kozarac, in Prijedor; and many more. Moving onto the month of June. Many killings included the notorious events such as the aforementioned killing of 77 Muslim men in Velagici; the killing of over 20 non-Serbs in front of the medical centre in Kotor Varos on the 25th of May; the killing of over 170 men at Gero's slaughtered house; the killing of about 20 men by members of the Yellow Wasps in the Celopek Dom Kultur; and many more. In July, you have heard evidence of the killing of 144 men in the Biljani school in Kljuc on the 10th of July; the killing of 180 non-Serbs in room 3 at Keraterm; and the killings of about 24 to 25 non-Serb men during transfer from Sanski Most to the Manjaca camp on 7th of July. I apologise. The hospital centre in Kotor Varos was in the month of June. In August, we have heard about the killing of about 200 non-Serbs transported from Trnopolje camp on the Vlasic mountain cliffs, also known as Koricanske Stijene as Koricanske Stijene; and we've heard of killings of Muslims and Croats at the Manjaca camp; and we have already heard of killings of non-Serbs on the Kotlina bridge in Gacko. In October, we have one last killing, this time at the building behind the SJB in Bileca. Your Honour, the fact speak volume about the determination of the Bosnian Serb leadership to remove Muslim and Croat civilians from Serb-held territories. Killings such as those we just glanced over serve two purposes: Physically destroying parts of the population which was intended to be removed and create an atmosphere of terror which would prompt the rest of the population to leave the area. Your Honours have already heard various accounts of attacks, armed attacks on non-Serbs -- non-Serb parts of town and villages. A cursory review of the evidence allows one to observe yet another pattern which would force Muslims and Croats to leave their homes. For example, on the 27th of May, the village of Pudin Han in Kljuc was heavily shelled killing a number of inhabitants as a consequence. Following the take-over the Doboj, the Muslim neighbourhood of Carsija was shelled on the 3rd of May damaging the main mosque. In Zvornik, you heard in the earlier video how the UN envoy reported the anti-aircraft cannons shelling from the Serbian side of the river into Muslim villages in Zvornik. In Visegrad, you heard how journalist Ian Traynor qualified the attack on the 13th of April in one of his articles. Referring to the arm he stated: "There is little doubt that they and the Serbian irregulars are moving in for the kill." He added in Court, still referring to the army and Serb paramilitary troops: "As we moved towards Visegrad, they were together. I was standing beside them as they were firing rockets into Visegrad both from artillery pieces." In Kotor Varos, we have had the chance to view a video showing the attack on Muslim parts of town by aeroplane showing the superiority of the equipment from the Serb forces. If we could see this video, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, for the record this is Exhibit P2014. Your Honours, as a result of persecutory measures, large numbers of Muslims and Croats left the Serb controlled area, and when they didn't leave on their own, the Serb leadership made sure to facilitate their departure by organising convoys of buses thereby expelling thousands of non-Serb civilians. In Sanski Most, between 3500 and 5.000 non-Serbs left as a result of the take-over in April 1992. In Kotor Varos out of 10.640 Croats, only a thousand remained following the take-over. And from 11.000 Muslims, only 4500 remained. Against Sulejman Crncalo explained to Your Honour that people were rounded up by the RS MUP to be placed on buses that left Pale in convoys. RS MUP policemen escorted the convoys. In late June, the number of Muslims from Pale were also transferred by buses. In Zvornik, quotes are attributed to a Serbian mayor, Brano Grujic, which provided chilling insight into the changing nature of that municipality from 1992. In 1993, he stated that: "The demographics are now different. Zvornik once had a population of almost 70.000 with more than 60 per cent being Muslims. Today, the mosque has been blown up and the city is more than 90 per cent Serb, maybe even 99 per cent." The next video will illustrate what forcible transfer and deportation means.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: "Some 2.000 people were unaccounted for. Nobody knows how many of them were executed on the spot or how many were sent to concentration camps where the murder continued. The rest were expelled. Forty-nine thousand Muslims lived in Zvornik. None remain. Five centuries of Islamic life and culture there were erased. This is ethnic cleansing. It became routine as the Serbs took control of three-quarters of Bosnia's territory. In time, they learned to keep the cameras out but ethnic cleansing continued."

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: This was Exhibit P908, Your Honours. In Bijeljina, you have heard evidence from Milorad Davidovic that one of the architects of this expulsion was the CSB chief, Predrag Jesuric, another one -- another one of these architects was Vojkan Jerkovic. Can play the next video-clip, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: "My guide was Vojkan Jerkovic, who was of Bijeljina's most prominent citizens. He was one of the 60 fighters who seized the town of the Serbs at the beginning of the war. Vojkan was especially proud of his expensive Italian sunglasses. Men like him are doing very well these days in the Bosnian Serb republic. At his office Vojkan had assembled some of the last Muslims left in Bijeljina. He said they're his friends. Vojkan is president of the regional commission for the free movement of the civilian population. That means is he in charge of ethnic cleansing. A report prepared for the UN said he has led groups of armed men had been terrorising the Muslim community. Vojkan cheerfully denies it all. "[No interpretation] "He has turned ethnic cleansing into an official procedure and turned Bijeljina into such an ethnically Serb town that these Muslims are desperate to get out. "[No interpretation]"

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: This is Exhibit P140, Your Honours. And another excerpt of this video Djurkovic claims that he should be receiving the Noble peace prize because he estimated that he had saved thousands of lives. Speaking of the Muslims he had just thrown out, he would go on to add these words: "They were tourists. We took a stroll from Bijeljina to Tuzla or to Berlin or somewhere else. Let them come back." Djurkovic was seen at Luka camp as was told to you by Isak Gasi. Banja Luka, Your Honours, resettlement agencies were also settled. And you have heard from Witness S225 [sic] the following: "Unfortunately those are the most tragic moments in the lives of us. Your friends, brothers, fathers, neighbours are leaving. Maybe the most difficult the citizens of Banja Luka went through during that period. And it went on and on, convoy after convoy, bus after bus. Very difficult good-byes from the assembly points where the citizens of Banja Luka went to get on the busses, and for those who stayed behind there was uncertainty, huge uncertainty as to what would become of them. If were to single out some moments from the overall tragedy in the area then I would choose this. These are very earth-shattering experiences." As adequately reported in a 1 KK report on the 1st of June, 1992, a portion of the Muslim and Croat population is moving out. Those departing will not be allowed to return. It's Exhibit P411.29. Your Honours have already heard throughout the trial that the homes and property of non-Serbs were systematically torched and destroyed. The limited time we have, Your Honours, here is a video of the result of attacks on the villages of Kozarac -- on the village of Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: "We visited the ethnically cleansed Kozarac in northern Bosnia last week. We were closely supervised by the local Serb militia restricted to just a few blocks of the town, once home to about 15.000 Muslim men, women, and children. Today there are no Muslims there; none. And none of their X-marked homes is in intact. Other homes in Kozarac have been marked to survive. This one with the colours of the Serbian flag. This one says, This is Serbia. They stand undamaged like the remaining Serb residents of Kozarac surrounded in silence, deadly silence."

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: This is Exhibit P1718. It was filmed in October 1992. It was highlighted by one witness, Your Honours, not a single Serb house had been attacked in Kozarac. Your Honours let's me conclude with these words. The Trial Chamber has received a great deal of evidence: Killings of Muslims and Croat civilians and inflexion of bodily harm in 1992 on a massive scale, and also received considerable evidence on atrocious conditions in detention facilities. We asked the Trial Chamber to keep in mind the considerable evidence about the forcible displacement and systematic transfer of the territory claimed by the Serbs. The Trial Chamber must assess the evidence in conjunction with the statements of the Bosnian Serb leadership anticipating the take-over of large parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the creation of ethnically pure areas. The intent of the Bosnian Serb leadership can be inferred from several aspects of the evidence, including the scale and the pattern of the attacks, their intensity, the substantial number of Muslims killed, the detention of Muslims and Croats, their brutal treatment in those detention facilities, destruction of their property. These are all factors that must be considered by the Trial Chamber. This concludes our presentation on the evidence of pattern. I will now leave the floor to Ms. Korner who will deal with the background of the creation of the RS MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Before you do so, Mr. Demirdjian, could you just clarify one thing. The video you showed with the aircrafts bombing some targets on land, when was that taken?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: July 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And you referred to Exhibit P2014.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: 2014, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But that appears to be an interview with Stojan Zupljanin, Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: It's a -- it's a video. It's a compellation of a video showing interviews. And interspersed in those videos, there are clippings that show the attacks. There are various attacks in that video. You also see soldiers carrying shells that are being fired towards mosques and inhabited areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I, as I explained earlier this morning, say a little bit about the background to the creation of the MUP because the Stanisic final brief devotes a number of pages to the testimony of the Serb members of the RS MUP and who had been formerly members of the BiH MUP and who gave their reasons to Your Honours for what could be said to be their disenchantment with the state of the BiH MUP between the beginning of 1991 and April of 1992. We would submit that obviously it's a one-sided view. For obvious reasons, Your Honours didn't hear from, really, any of the Muslim members of the BiH MUP except very briefly those who were victims. It is said in paragraph 44 of the brief that the recitation of the background of the events provides the context and reasons for the split in the MUP which took place at the beginning of April 1992. Well, Your Honours, can we make one thing absolutely clear. There is no dispute in this case that after the 1990 elections the HDZ, the SDA, and the SDS entered into an agreement on the divisions of posts that was to take place amongst their separate nominees, governmental posts and MUP posts. In the MUP, the minister, of course, was Delimustafic, who was SDA or Muslim; the deputy minister, Mr. Zepinic; and the under-secretary for the SDB was a Croat named Kvesic. And it is equal not disputed at all that this so-called agreement led to, in fact, a number of disagreements and much arguing about personnel and positions and who had what. The complaints which were rehearsed, as a result of questions from the Defence by nearly all the witnesses which are repeated in the final trial brief, was that the Serb police were being marginalised, that this was the fault of the SDA, that unqualified Muslims from Sandzak were being recruited, the inequities of persons such as Mr. Hebib and Mr. Alibabic, all of those complaints, in fact, were being made in June 1991 by a Serb ex-employee of the MUP named Goran Zecevic. It's P517. And Your Honours can see some excerpts from that document. It's addressed to the council of the SDS, and talks about -- what aggrieves my colleagues is that the SDS lost the secretariat of the interior positions that should have been following to them. Key positions in the MUP have been occupied by the SDA and the HDZ and the leading figure in the MUP is the minister. And it goes on, and I don't think I need bother to go through the other parts of the documents, though we have it up to, as I say, rehearse the complaints which were then rehearsed by all of these witnesses. What is not referred to at all in the final trial brief is the report on the ethnic structure of the ministry which was prepared, and Your Honours we haven't put that up, but it's P829. And testimony that was actually given by Mr. Mandic in the Krajisnik case, and Your Honours can I just remind you of this. It was, although Mr. Mandic resiled from some of his testimony, either voluntarily before he testified but after he had seen the Defence or later, as a result from questions of the Defence, he did not resile from this, and this is page 8650 of his previous testimony which is P1318.2. And he was asked: "Mr. Mandic, did some of the steps towards the preparation for separation of the joint MUP or unified MUP include arming of Serbian police stations or police officials and at least the beginnings of the terminations of non-Serbs from police forces? Mandic relied this: "Well, I think it was the other way round then. Up until the beginning of the war, in the police of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there were about 11.000 members of the MUP. From among them, there were 75 per cent Serbs. In Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was mainly Serbs who were in the army and police which did not correspond to the ethnic pattern of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So conclusions were reached by the senior staff of the MUP to dismiss Serb personnel who were trained and educated to work on this kind of job and that Bosniaks and Croats should be recruited from elsewhere, including the reserve force, and the Territorial Defence, so that the pattern would correspond with the ethnic pattern in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That means, at that time, there were more Serbs on the force than there were in Bosnia-Herzegovina itself and that is one of the problems that was faced by the joint MUP." That evidence does not get a mention in the final trial brief. Your Honours, equally, if we look, please, at P905, this was a letter that was sent protesting about Mr. Mandic and his work to all and sundry -- when I say "all and sundry," I mean Mr. Izetbegovic, Mr. Delimustafic, Mr. Zepinic, Mr. Hebib. And if we look, please, at the next part of the slide, we are writing this letter in respect of the work and behaviour of the assistant minister, Mr. Mandic, who has put him in charge of personnel policy an oddly enough his speciality is being the selection and bringing on board of Muslim employees without anybody's -- concerned. So the complaints that are made by the Serb that you heard from about Muslims being brought on were apparently also being brought on by Mr. Mandic. And it goes on to say: "On the other hand, when it comes to the Serbian personnel the wishes and orders of the SDS and Mr. Karadzic are fully respected with no questions asked." And finally this kind of work is explained by Mr. Mandic's good relationship with the minister of the interior, Mr. Delimustafic, which originates from their joint business ventures: "We demand that Mr. Mandic be urgently prevented in his actions and intentions and that all remaining vacancies in the BH MUP that belong to the SDA cadre as per the inter-party agreement be filled but without Mr. Mandic's interference." So, Your Honours, the -- these complaints about who was doing what, who was interfering with what, were common to all parties and all sides, and it was not the one-sided issue, if one likes to put it that way, that the many of the witnesses and, indeed, the brief would have you believe. Additionally, not mentioned, is the October 1991 paper, the possibilities of organising a Serbian MUP Ministry for Internal Affairs, again, not going to trouble to put it up, but, Your Honours, it's P521. Moreover, it's the reaction by Karadzic, the leader of the SDS, to these arguments over personnel in 1991 was unequivocal. We just look for a moment at part of an intercept which is P897, a conversation in July of 1991, all arising out of arguments over who had what ministry. Karadzic, in terms, saying to Zepinic: "Let the collegium meet every morning. I was with Izetbegovic last night and Zulfikarpasic and I told him right into his face, We'll establish a parallel government, parallel police, we'll withdraw our people and they'll have to be paid by the government. We withdraw all our people under arms. We'll establish an entire parallel state if you keep on screwing us." Et cetera. And again, at P903, another intercept. Karadzic and Simovic in September: "Tell Zepinic that as of tomorrow we are withdrawing all our ministers and all our officials in the MUP. We are discontinuing the complete partnership and going in opposition. Vlaski," whom Your Honours heard from, "was removed from his office and it's over. Tonight at 8.00 I'm going to break up with Izetbegovic. I'm withdrawing everything. Serbian Democratic Party into opposition. We're going to break apart and then we are going to establish our own SUP separately, and with other men and we'll make the government separately. We'll make everything separately." Your Honours, it may well be that nobody took Karadzic's threats that seriously in that part of 1991. In fact, it was their mistake, we submit, and they should have taken those threats seriously. Your Honours, moreover, we do not quite follow, if that's the right word, the Defence's train of thought on this. Because the Defence case is that there simply never was any plan to split the BiH MUP. The only time that it became under -- that it came under active consideration was at the result of the Cutileiro agreement that Your Honours have heard so much about. In the Stanisic final brief, between paragraphs 98 and 119, that is the position that they adopt, in which case it is not easy to see why this background has any relevance to the split which took place, except as, we say, for what was being said by Karadzic at a very early stage. In fact, with respect to the Cutileiro Plan, Your Honours, the evidence shows that even before the declaration of the Serbian state in BiH in January of 1992 and long before the Cutileiro talks got started in February, the split in the MUP was being planned and planned secretly. On the 19th of December, one has what's been called the Variant A and B instructions. And, Your Honours, those were referred to by Karadzic in his speech at the 50th Assembly meeting in 1995. And Your Honours will see an extract from that speech on the screen where, "And we really start. We mobilise then, we did not have a war." Ten lines down: "At the moment the war began, in the municipalities where we were in the majority, we had municipal power, held it firmly, controlled everything. In the municipalities where we were in the minority, we set up secret government, municipal boards, municipal assemblies, presidents. You will remember, the A and B variants. In the B variant where we were in the minority, we had set up a government and a brigade," and so on and so forth. And then he deals with the involvement of the JNA. The war began and the JNA helped as much as it could here and there. It had helped before. He adds he hopes he isn't going out on television this. General Subotic helped just before the war began by sending the tanks, took the risk, signed for them to go to servicing while, in fact, he sent them to Banja. Banja, yeah. And then it was -- he talks about the fall of one of the other municipalities done with the help of Subotic who was a colonel here.
