Distribution of weapons was carried out, thanks to the JNA, and so on and so forth. And then, at the bottom: "It was the SDS which organised the people and created the army. It was an army. Together with the police, those were the armed forces of the Serbian Republic and Bosnia and Herzegovina. They created the space, they [sic] liberated and created the space." And, Your Honours, of course, that is the Prosecution case in a nutshell, that the police were the armed force, and together, once the VRS was created, did just that: Liberated, if that's the word, the territories. Your Honours going back to why we say the split in the MUP was already being planned well before the Cutileiro talks. On the 21st of December, 1991, the council of ministers, as part of this parallel shadow government, was created. And at that state Zepinic was named as minister of the interior. And that's P180. Then we come to the 11th of February meeting in Banja Luka. Can we just have that up for a moment. Now, Your Honours, it is asserted by all the witnesses who Your Honours heard from who attended the meeting, including Mr. Mandic, in particular, that there's no way this was a secret meeting. Mr. Mandic asserted that he even spoke to Mr. Delimustafic about it. History in the form of Mr. Mandic, does not relate what Mr. Delimustafic's response to this invitation was. We suggest that in that respect, Mr. Mandic was not telling the truth at all. None of the other witnesses appear to be able to explain how they had ever got an invitation to this meeting in the first place, or nobody could remember, and if this was an open meeting, open to anyone, there wasn't a single non-Serb person there. The meeting was not held in the CSB Banja Luka despite the fact that Your Honours saw the CSB Banja Luka had ample rooms to hold the meeting. Your Honours saw the photographs through one of the witnesses. Having said that, Your Honour, it's a matter for Your Honours to decide whether this was, firstly, a meeting that was being kept quiet; and, secondly, whether it was a pivotal meeting in the split of the MUP. But, clearly, Stanisic's speech said, Work has to be done by the organisation of the Serbian MUP, starting from the municipal and regional levels, up to the Serbian ministry. The Serbian personnel in the MUP must provide the means to strengthen and supply the Serbian MUP, ensuring that resources will be distributed equally. And if one looks very briefly at what each of the -- some of the participants say in turn: "Bjelosevic: I support the decision to establish the Serbian MUP. "Zugic: The Serbian MUP has to start work as soon as possible. "Jesuric: I only trust my own people and weapons that I have acquired and hidden, the Serbian MUP should be established as soon as possible." Two further quotes: "Mr. Vlaski: The only -- who also denied that this was a meeting concerned with splitting the MUP. The only way would be to organise the Serbian MUP and implement all decisions without question. "Mr. Draskovic: This is the first time that we are telling each other the truth without the people who have been holding us back." And finally, Your Honours, in the conclusions suggested that Mr. Delimustafic was going to be sent, the conclusions of the meeting, that's not in fact what happened because if you look at the conclusions: "The Serbian collegium of the MUP is hereby instructed to carry out all preparations necessary for the functioning of the Serbian MUP, after the promulgation of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia constitution." And no mention in any of the conclusions of sending Mr. Delimustafic -- the conclusions. Your Honour, the next important meeting that took place was that of the SDS in Holiday Inn on the 14th of February, and there Karadzic explained not only that whilst the Serbs and the Croats wanted the cantons, he was discussing the talks that had gone on, and the Muslims want a unitary Bosnia-Herzegovina, but also that under no circumstances were any Serbs to participate in any referendum. The second level of the Variant A and B instructions were to be implemented, and he added: "As for the army and the defence of the Serbian Krajina, we will anticipate everything: The police we will make a plan of defence and security operations." An and that's P1841. Your Honours, we say that from the moment the SDS had made its decision that there was to be a separate Serbian state in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the formation of its own security forces, both army and police, was a foregone conclusion. And it was one, we say, that was evident to all of the senior MUP officials who attended the February meeting in Banja Luka. Your Honours, can I move, then, very shortly to mention one other aspect of -- of the -- which has come out through the Defence cross-examination. Your Honours, throughout the trial, the Defence have attempted and sometimes succeeded in introducing evidence of events which are outside the scope of the indictment, outside the period, in the interests of what they've called context. So that, for example, Your Honours have heard about the alleged secret training in Croatia of Muslim and Croat police officers. Your Honours that's covered in the Stanisic final brief between paragraph 62 and 69. Can I just sort of, out of interest, put -- ask for one document to be put up from this series that related to the training. That's 1D787. Now, Your Honours, this was put -- oh, it's gone. For some reason, it's gone blank on my screen. Anyhow. Yes, thank you. Your Honours, this -- this is a document that was put in by the Defence as part of this series of documents showing training going on in Croatia. This is June of 1991. But Your Honours it does show and indeed Mr. Nilsson dealt with this to a certain extent in his report that these were rumours that's -- that was supposed to be secret training - but in actual fact was ordinary training conducted, and don't forget at this stage Yugoslavia as such still existed - containing a number of different ethnic groups. And if one looks at the list of people here and the commanders it would appear that they were indeed mixed, Your Honours, between certainly, apparently, Serbs and, in this particular instant, Croats. So we suggest that the so-called secret training should again be looked at with a degree of skepticism. Your Honours also heard about events in Bosanski Brod, in Derventa, about Muslim attempts to procure arms, about Crisis Staffs being formed by the SDA and the HDZ, and about crimes being committed by Muslims or Croats against Serbs. Many of the insider witnesses, the Serb witnesses, were very insistent in having their say about what they said were the crimes committed against the Serbs. Your Honours, the -- as -- some of which was adduced by Defence counsel. Witnesses ST-19 was asked the following series of questions by Mr. Pantelic. It's at page -- it's T593: "Q. Witness, which forces killed hundreds upon hundreds of Serbs in Kotor Varos municipality? Do you know? "A. No, I don't know. "Q. Who roasted living Serbs in Kotor Varos municipality? Do you know that? "A. No. "Q. Who burned and levelled the Serb villages in the territory of Kotor Varos municipality. Do you know? "A. I don't. "Q. No further questions for this witness." Your Honour, that's an extreme example, but, nonetheless, it is something that was adduced through the Defence. Your Honours, because of -- this trial involves these two accused and because the evidence that has been led is that which relates to their involvement, Your Honours have no real opportunity to examine the type of evidence that was adduced in its proper context. And the Defence that at one stage it seemed was being mounted, namely that all the actions taken by the Serbs were nothing more than self-defence is not, in fact, sought to be advanced, nor, on the evidence could it have been in the context of the events of 1992. And it may not need saying, but out of an abundance of caution we say it: It is not a Defence to say that the other side committed crimes and so we were justified in committing the crimes that we did. Revenge attacks, which is something that's being mentioned often, are still crimes. Your Honours, finally before I turn to the question of resubordination, can I just talk very briefly about joint criminal enterprise, Mr. Pantelic's favour topic. Neither accused, in fact, seek to argue in their final trial briefs that the crimes alleged did not take place. In fact, in paragraph 219 of the Zupljanin brief, it's said in terms, nor, with a few exceptions, namely, the special police actions in Kotor Varos, do they seek to argue that the police did not take part in crimes. The evidence is overwhelming on that matter. Neither accused further seeks to argue in their final brief that a joint criminal enterprise did not exist. We say that is because the evidence of such an enterprise is overwhelming, not only from what was said at the time and subsequently by members of the Serb political, military, and police leadership, but also by the pattern so clearly demonstrated in the address given to you by Mr. Demirdjian of the events in the indictment. Your Honours, that the enterprise had, as its object, the forcible removal of the non-Serbs from the territory of the Serbian state, we say, is absolutely clear. And if there were no other evidence but that of the six strategic goals, that would set it out. And, Your Honours, can we look at the version not that given on the 12th of May by Karadzic in the Assembly but by the note made by General Mladic on the 7th of May, so five days before the Assembly, of his discussions with Krajisnik, where the strategic goals are set out. And goal number 1 is: To separate from the Croats and Muslims forever. And then the further goals of the corridor from the Krajina; the Drina, Neretva -- I'll redo that one. Neretva with -- Nere -- anyways, I give that one up. Even after all this time. A natural border with the Croats. And then a part of Sarajevo is to be ours. The Muslims can have their part of the city and a link with their territory. Then the passage to the sea. And links with the Republika of Serb Krajina. Your Honour, the issue in this case is really were the two accused members of the JCE. Both of them deny it. They deny any knowledge of the crimes committed. They say, as a result of the lack of communication from their subordinates and/or the faulty communications equipment, and Mr. Hannis will deal with that as a separate topic a little later, and, to a certain extent they blame interference from municipal authorities, in particular the Crisis Staffs. Not surprisingly, Zupljanin is running an alternative Defence and sets it out as an alternative in a number of different place, that if he did know of the crimes, they fell outwith his responsibility as, at the time, the perpetrators, if they were members of the MUP, were all resubordinated to the VRS. Of course, Your Honours, the essence of the joint criminal enterprise is that all involved had a role to play and notwithstanding that the course of the relationships between the political, the army and the police did not always run smoothly, in the end, as a number of witnesses said, they did share the same goal. The MUP at all times was and had to be an integral component of any plant to take over and retain territory. In every municipality that Your Honours saw this morning, one of the first actions was the take-over of the SJB. Before the creation of the VRS on the 12th of May, the only armed force on which the Bosnian Serbs could positively rely was the MUP because at that stage they did not know even if the JNA was secretly arming, secretly prepared to help, they could not know whether or not the JNA would come down on their side in any conflict, would, as they did, provide manpower and materiel to carry on the -- the plan. And so the only armed force at the beginning, until May, and Your Honours saw how many of the take-overs happened before May, was the MUP. We say it is inconceivable that the head of the MUP, who, in this case, was, we say, was a member of the SDS, although it is denied, had been a part of the shadow government from no later than December 1991, together with the head of the police in the largest targeted area for the Serbian state should have been no more than the innocent tools, which is what it comes down to, of a Machiavellian Bosnian Serb political leadership. The removal of Zepinic, who was, after all, chosen to be the first minister of the interior in the shadow government, shows the importance, we submit, that was attached to having a head of the MUP who was prepared to carry out the enterprise. And, Your Honours, as we have shown, we submit, through the evidence, as set out in our final trial brief, both of the accused, Stanisic and Zupljanin, played their parts in the implementation of the criminal enterprise. Your Honours, can I now, very briefly, before I move to Zupljanin, turn to the vexed question of resubordination. The accused - and in particular Zupljanin because he was closer to the perpetrators of the crime in his position as chief of CSB - rely on what is described by them as the principle of resubordination. Namely, that of all relevant times when crimes were committed by members of the MUP as we have shown they were, they were under the command and control of the army, the VRS. And they say that in order to assert that this deprived them of effective control of their subordinates. Your Honours, the focus at this stage is not going to be on the power to prevent or punish being removed from the accused - Mr. Olmsted will deal with that tomorrow - but on the evidence as to whether or not this resubordination actually took place. Your Honours, for one last time, or maybe more, if the Defence are going to let us have a look, please, at Article 10 far -- 104 of the Law of All People's Defence, which is in L1. Your Honours, the word "resubordination" does not appear in the Article. It says: "In war, in times of an immediate threat of war and ... other emergencies, the police may," emphasising the word "may," "... be used for carrying out combat activities for the armed forces in accordance with the law." We submit the word "may" makes it clear that this is intended to be the exception and not the rule. And then: "During its engagement for combat activities in the armed forces the police shall be under the command of the authorised officer in charge of combat activity." I'm not sure -- we put it onto the slide, but, Your Honour, it goes on to say: "The reserve forces of the police shall be reinforced by military conscripts." Now, Your Honours, we submit that because, as Your Honours know, that the great theory of Defence expert Kovacevic is that -- that -- that everybody is a military conscript in a time of immediate threat of war. Your Honours, it's clear here that there is a distinction made between a military conscript and the police. Now, it is the evidence from one of the military witnesses who had actual experience of the conflict during 1992 was that to use the police for combat operations which, according to one witness, meant being on the front line, and we suggest that is the obvious common sense meaning of combat in the context of Article 104. A formal process had to be gone through which involved seeking approval from a senior officer who in turn would have to request the use of MUP units from the appropriate MUP level. And by Stanisic's order of the 14th of May, that would be the CSB chief. Moreover, it was a procedure of limited duration, geography, and purpose. Now, there is no doubt the evidence shows there were police units who were actually resubordinated. The police brigade which was set up by Zupljanin in 1992, November of 1992, was clearly a police units that had been resubordinated to the military for the purposes of action. But, as expressed in at least one report, such resubordination was, as it's put, occasional. This is P163, the meeting of the Trebinje working group in August, where the chief of the Doboj CSB mentioned the possibility of a conflict between the army and the MUP, regarding, in the view of the army members, the privileged war-time position of MUP employees in relation to them. And, Your Honours, that one has a classic example of the relationship not always running smoothly. He therefore suggested that the reserve police force and the soldiers on the front line alternate tours of duties or that the reserve police force is occasionally subordinated to the army. Now, Your Honours, there were obviously instances where strict procedures weren't followed and this particularly, we would suggest depended on the relationship between the local police, MUP commander, and the VRS officer. If it was a good relationship, or the VRS officer had a particularly overbearing nature, then, it was clear that the proper procedures were sometimes by-passed and it's worth -- again, I hope one last time, looking at the Lisica/Bjelosevic correspondence. Can we have a look at 1D263, please, or part thereof. This was Mr. Bjelosevic writing to, as he then was, Colonel Lisica, and saying that -- he is complaining. It's not on the screen but he is complaining about the robberies, and so on and so forth, and he says: "In order to prevent these occurrences, we are forced to withdraw the police from combat operations on the fronts in Bosanski Brod and Gradacac. We will carry out the withdrawal of the police from these fronts ..." Now, Your Honours, the plain meaning of this is: This is what I'm going to do. This is not a request. This is what I'm going to do. And then we hope that you will understand the reasons why we are forced to withdraw the police from the battle-field. Expect your positive reply. So we get the next -- letter back the following -- that's the 2nd of October, the 3rd of October, from Colonel Lisica who, as Your Honours, know takes the view that in time of war, whether declared or undeclared, he's the boss. And whether or not the regulations agree -- that. I do not authorise the withdraw of the police forces, because if I do so, the front will soon reach Doboj and you will not have any territory under your control. If you'll correctly understand the reasons why the police forces cannot be withdrawn. We welcome all forms of co-operation and assistance between the military police and the police force. In fact, he's probably making -- Your Honours, making a fairly sensible point, that if there is fighting going on there the police are better off staying with him. And then on the 6th of October, Bjelosevic replies and says: "I was rather surprised by the content of the order, all the more since I believe that co-operation between the TG 3 and the Doboj CSB has been excellent." And, Your Honours, we say that is the operative word, "co-operation." And then if we go further on, we skipped about official vehicles being put in his disposal: "While I was issuing approval for the engagement of the police in combat ... outside my authorisation and the order of the minister of the interior, there was looting and disorder on a massive scale." Your Honours, we suggest that, again, we have the CSB chief giving approval and he, himself, says because of his relationship with presumably Colonel Lisica, he had by-passed the chain of command which ought to have taken place. And, as we say, we accept the evidence is plain that sometimes the proper procedures were not gone through but all were aware of those procedures and resubordination was not, as Zupljanin Defence [indiscernible] would have you believe an automatic thing as they say. The army was there, then the police were resubordinated. It was a highly technical matter. Your Honours, in order to overcome the plain fact that not one of the crimes charged in which members of the MUP were involved, is there any evidence at all to suggest that the police who were involved were part of a resubordinated unit. The Defence are, in fact, forced to try and extend what we say was a formal short-lived action to encompass all police action taken in an area which contained a military unit under the principle that you have heard over and over again of singleness or unity of command, which is a military term, and certainly applies if there are resubordinated units properly resubordinated. But it does not, we suggest, on the evidence, encompass every single action in which the police or the military co-ordinated or co-operated. Your Honours, all of the undisputed actions by the police, the crimes that were committed, the looting, the destruction, the killings that took place after events such as the shelling of Kozarac, or Mahala, the suffocation of the prisoners on the truck who had been brought by the police to Manjaca as is evidenced in the report from one of the persons at Manjaca, the guarding of prisoners in camps which have no military presence whatsoever, as demonstrated to you by Mr. Demirdjian, all of that, it is asserted, took place whilst the police officers involved were resubordinated. And it's asserted that the words "co-operation" and "co-ordination" all imply that a relationship of resubordination existed. Well, Your Honours, if we look for a moment at P60.3, this was the order given to -- I believe it's Lieutenant-Colonel Peulic, that he was to move his troops and, as it is put: "Establish full co-operation with the organs of the government in Sanski Most municipality and collaboration with the To and police units." Now this was shown to the Defence expert who said that means -- although it's difficult because I don't know the background, but in my view that means resubordination. Your Honours can I just go to private session for one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And we now take the break and resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I finish fairly swiftly, I keep saying because of the time constraints, the question of resubordination. Your Honour, no doubt, many of the insider witnesses from the MUP supported the population that resubordination virtually occurred anywhere where there is army and police. They, of course, would say so, as we submit, out of self-interest. It deflects any attention from their activities at the time and, of course, the Defence expert, Kovacevic, about whom Your Honours know we have already made lengthy submissions. In fact, the OTP rely on the documents that came into existence at the time and on the evidence of what happened. Mr. Brown, as I've already mentioned, receives a barrage of criticism, much of it being through selective misquoting, particularly in the Zupljanin final brief, and we say that paragraph 250 requires careful reading, but the OTP do not rely heavily on him for this aspect of the case; because, as he pointed out, it was not the focus of his report and the research which he carried out which was on the activities of the VRS in the Krajina area during 1992 and not the nature of the relationship between the police and the military. He was, of course, asked about it because by the stage at which he testified, the issue had become clear, which, as we say, was definitely not made clear before the start of this trial. Your Honour, we say those documents show and we have set them out far fuller in our final brief. First, that the VRS accepted that there needed to be a request before they could have the police resubordinated. We rely on, for example, document 1D641. Then if Your Honours also look at P1789 and footnote 3076. The RS MUP themselves refused or restricted requests; for example, P376. The VRS themselves distinguished between co-ordinated action and resubordination. It's set out -- the documents are set out in the footnote to our brief 3066. And the RS MUP in its annual report referred specifically to combat activities at the front line. If Your Honours note, is P625 at page 8, also 1D406. And we invite Your Honours to look at paragraph 237 of the Zupljanin final brief. Your Honour, in no document produced at the time is there any suggestion that in every activity connected with the take-overs or their aftermath in which the members of the RS MUP were engaged that at all times and in all places they were not under the authority of their superiors in the MUP, but, rather, resubordinated units who were under the authority of the army. That suggestion is not made. And, in fact, it couldn't have been, because, as Your Honours have heard this morning, at the time of take-overs, for example, in Bijeljina and in Zvornik, there was no VRS. There was no Serb army. There was only the JNA, which, of course, did engage in those take-overs. Your Honour, some time is spent in both briefs on the question of town commands. Your Honours will also have seen our submission on that. We say they have almost no bearing at all on the events in this indictment. Indeed, in Kotor Varos, where apparently some kind of a town command was supposed to be established, and was established, the Crisis Staff was operating throughout the period until November 1992 when the last stronghold of Muslim resistance, Vecici, fell to the Serbs. Your Honour, the last topic on that that I want to deal with are -- is this percentages which the Defence have raised. Your Honours, the accused at various times, have suggested that 80 per cent of the RS MUP was resubordinated at any one time and at one stage, Mr. Stanisic was suggesting to the government that there was 100 per cent of the MUP engaged in Herzegovina which is the Trebinje CSB and in Doboj. Your Honours, we don't have figures from Doboj but we have figures from the other reports. And, Your Honours, we've put them up on the screen, we hope, in an attempt to assist. Your Honours, the MUP -- sorry. The Banja Luka year-end report, P624, and this is the document on which the percentages is put by Mr. Krgovic, I believe, to Mr. Macar were taken from. And there they say it should be mentioned that 5034 employees were engaged in combat operations for 114.529 days, and that's the basis of the 80 per cent calculation. This works out to an average of 23 days of combat per police employee for that nine-month period. It doesn't indicate -- it just says engaged in combat and it doesn't indicate whether the police were resubordinated during these operations. We say it's made clear in other documents that resubordination and police involvement in combat are not synonymous. In addition to participating independently in combat operations - and there you have it, Your Honours - the police also made 1.593 reserve on a 39 activity duty police employees available to the Army of Republika Srpska, and we say there's a clear distinction being made there, being made available, being resubordination independently not being resubordination. Your Honour, what we say is that it shows that only 1.632 police officers, both active and reserve, from the CSB Banja Luka area of responsibility were resubordinated during the -- to the VRS during combat operations between April and December and the rest them were participating, whatever that may be, independently but certainly not resubordinated. Mr. Krgovic used the CSB's December figures for active and reserve police within the CSB Banja Luka and we say that those figures are set out there, 1203 active and 5065 reserve; 31.5 per cent of the reserve police force and 3.2 of the activity police force during this period were resubordinated. And if we go to the next slide which deals with Trebinje, which is where Stanisic was apparently saying there were 100 resubordinated, that document which is P169, shows that the participation of active and reserve police within the CSB Trebinje in combat operations varied from month to month. That's on page 2. 482 officers participated in May. Between 176 and 181 participated in July and August. So based on the October figures for the reserve, which are shown as 530, and active, 192, within CSB Trebinje, that shows 67 per cent in May, 25 in July, and 46 per cent in October. The report doesn't indicate how they were participating, whether as resubordinated or independently. Your Honours, that's all that we wish to say about resubordination at this stage. Mr. Olmsted is going to say a little about it when he addresses you on the failures tomorrow. Your Honours, may I turn now to the role of Zupljanin. Again, because of the time constraints we are not going to go through everything that we have said in the brief about him, nor would it be of assistance, we feel, to Your Honour, who can, as I've always been told, read documents the way that I can. We say that the evidence that Zupljanin knowingly and with intent played a key role in the implementation of the joint criminal enterprise is overwhelming. He and the other CSB chiefs were the intermediate level of authority between the SJB chiefs and their police who were the actual perpetrators of the crimes and the RS MUP top echelon. Now, on his behalf, Your Honours, and this is what we're going to concentrate on, really three aspects of Zupljanin, that is raised by him in the final brief. It is contended, first, he was never a member of the SDS. He never attended any of their meetings. He did not conform to the party line and at one stage was apparently threatened. Those submissions appear in paragraphs 50, 55, and 104. Second, he was only a member of the ARK Crisis Staff (ex officio) - and I'll come back to that in a minute - for a matter of weeks during May. And that's paragraph 53. He never discriminated against non-Serbs; paragraph 15. He had nothing to do with the formation of the special police from the CSB Banja Luka or the absorption into the special police of members of the SOS. He had no authority or control over the actions of the special police. That's in paragraphs 15 and 171 to 216 inclusive. He did not order forces to participate in joint operations with the VRS. All police taking part in joint operations were subordinated. He knew nothing about the existence of any camps, particularly those in Prijedor until he was informed by Radulovic a short time before he attended the 11th of July meeting. And, finally, if he found out about crimes, he took prompt action, if he was able to, but, for the most part, he was unaware of those crimes. In other words, Your Honours, if one were to accept that throughout this whole period when Zupljanin was sitting in the CSB Banja Luka or out and about, as we know that he was, visiting the various areas within his area of responsibility, he was effectively cocooned in a ivory tower because that is what Defence submissions amount to. Can I just then please concentrate on three aspects of what they say. The first is his relationship with the SDS. There is no direct evidence, unlike, as we say, in respect of Stanisic, that he was ever a member of the SDS. But we say it is clear that he shared their ideals and in the multi-party jostling for positions in 1991 he was supported by local SDS leaders; for example, Brdjanin, in his capacity as president of the Celinac SDS. And that's P1098.12. Witness ST-174 believed that he was a member of the SDS. At paragraph 58 of the Zupljanin final brief, quotes what he says at transcript page 8135, but entirely omits the previous lines of his testimony and indeed, the statement he made in which he asserted that it was his belief if not his knowledge that Zupljanin was a member of the SDS, and his statement is Exhibit P1098.6. He was undoubtedly in contact with both Karadzic and Plavsic in 1991. He is described as "our man," and that's in P1178. And contrary to what is suggested, Your Honours, that he never attended any meetings of the SDS, there is strong circumstantial evidence to suggest that he both attended the Bosnian Serb Assembly on the 26th of January with the declaration of their state, and the Holiday Inn meeting on the 14th of February. He definitely attended the Bosnian Serb Assembly in October of 1992 in Prijedor because he is on video there and that will be shown to Your Honours later when Mr. Hannis addresses you about Stanisic. But can I just deal with his attendance at the Bosnian Serb Assemblies. Can we look first, please, at part of P1190. This is an intercept of a conversation -- in fact, I think it is wrongly titled. Zupljanin doesn't, himself, appear on the conversation. It's between Cizmovic, described as an unknown male, and Karadzic. It's on the 25th of January and there you will see that Cizmovic and Karadzic the day before the Bosnian-Serb Assembly. "Karadzic: Will we see each other at the theatre? "Cizmovic: We will but Stojan is asking if he should say. "Karadzic: Pardon? "Cizmovic: Stojan Zupljanin is asking if he should stay. Should he stay on a for tomorrow?" And Karadzic says: "That would be good." And that would seem to suggest, as we say, that he was there for the 26th of January meeting. We turn next to the 14th of February. We say there is no doubt he was there. On the 13th of February, Cizmovic again -- can I just remind Your Honours, Cizmovic was the so-called co-ordinator of the -- if the regions appointed back in December of 1991 and was actually a Banja Luka lawyer. Is, actually, a Banja Luka lawyer. Cizmovic saying to Karadzic on the 13th of February: "Can we meet earlier tomorrow, and Stojan would like to come with me? "Karadzic: I hope so. "Cizmovic: Where should we look for you? At the headquarters or -- "Karadzic: We'll be there. We'll have breaks so we'll have an opportunity to get together." This is the meeting which I reminded Your Honours of earlier this morning where Karadzic is describing the negotiations to assemble members of the SDS and the implementation of level two of the Variant A and B instructions. Can we look now, please, at P1353.17. Those who came from outside the Sarajevo area apparently stayed at the Holiday Inn -- a number of people. This is one of the receipts, and we say that receipt is that for Mr. Zupljanin. So we say it is untrue to assert that he never attended any of their meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Is there a date?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is there a?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: A date indicated on the bill.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Do you see to the right-hand side, Your Honour, says arrival 14.2 and departure 15.2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And we also have wrong translation as well. It says Supljanin, not Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: We also have wrong translation. It said he is Supljanin, not Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, well, Your Honours, so that's the -- thank you. We then come to the 2nd of March and the barricades incident in Sarajevo. Could we have look, please, at P981. This is a conversation between Zupljanin and then Stanisic. And if we go -- whose called by apparently appears to be his nickname, Stole, and Zupljanin tells him: "We're listens to how things are going over there. We are waiting for further instructions." Stanisic says: "You are in contact with this policy of yours, aren't you? "All right, now be ready. "For the most part everything is ready on our side. "Yes. Zupljanin: We are waiting for the sign. If a total blockade is needed or the rest, it will be done. "Agreed." Now, Your Honours, we say this shows that even if not a formal member of the SDS, he was certainly by March a party to the planning that was going on, and, indeed, from February at least for the meeting. Now, the -- his membership of the ARK Crisis Staff. Now, Your Honours, even before the announcement of the ARK Crisis Staff, as Zupljanin was, in fact, attending and reporting to the ARK Assembly. And that's P2061. He is listed as a member of the ARK Crisis Staff on the document P556, and, indeed, in the gazette that was published of all the ARK decisions up to June. Now, the Defence position on his membership of the ARK Crisis Staff, I think the fairest way of putting this is to say it has vacillated somewhat. In the pre-trial brief, at paragraphs 18 -- I'm just going to find it. This is the supplementary pre-trial brief that was filed on the 31st of July, 2009. And they say at paragraph 18: "Mr. Zupljanin also takes issue with the allegation that he was an active member of the ARK Crisis Staff and instrumental in the implementation of the alleged plan. In reality, his role was minor, and he did not have any influence upon the ARK Crisis Staff which was directed and controlled by Radoslav Brdjanin." At paragraphs 25, it is said: "The Crisis Staffs, War Presidencies, and War Presidents," I think they mean war staff, "were interchangable nomenclatures for the same institution." Well interestingly enough, Your Honours, that is not what was being put to Ms. Hanson who testified about this. What was there being put was that they were completely different institutions. Indeed, I think at that stage when this was being dealt with, I actually got up and asked - it's fair to say it was Mr. Pantelic - whether the suggestion was by the Defence that there was a totally separate body called a war staff from the ARK Crisis Staff which was simply Mr. Brdjanin alone without any participation by Mr. Zupljanin. Is that the suggestion and the answer was, Yes, that is my suggestion. And that is at T4647. The paragraph 25 of the pre-trial brief, goes on to say: "Mr. Zupljanin takes issue with the contention that the ARK Crisis Staff issued decisions which were sent to municipal Crisis Staffs and put into effect. The municipal Crisis Staffs were neither charged to do so nor did they do so, in fact. " Well, as Your Honours will see in the brief now there is a change, because it said not originally but later on the ARK Crisis Staff did have power over the municipal Crisis Staff. And, finally, at paragraph 33 they repeat the suggestion that Mr. Zupljanin's role in that organ was negligible and his acts and conduct did not have any impact on the creation of either orders and discussions or the outcome alleged." Well, Your Honour it is now said that in fact he was only a member of the ARK Crisis Staff for the period of May. Your Honours, there is -- that's what's asserted. There is absolutely no evidence at all that that is in fact the situation. The ARK Crisis Staff went from May until the 17th of July, and there's nothing to suggest that Zupljanin as various witnesses have attested did attend those meetings of the Crisis Staff as a member. Your Honour, the words ex officio are used in both of the accused's briefs. My understanding or our understanding of ex officio is that by virtue of the characteristics inherent in the holding of a particular office you hold an appointment without need of specific authorisation or specific appointment. In the case of the SJB chiefs, and Zupljanin, they were on the Crisis Staffs by direction of the government. Can we look brief, please, at P70, this is Djeric's order. The Crisis Staff consists of members, each of whom has his own responsibilities: The president, et cetera et cetera, head of the MUP. It is not clear either, Your Honours may think, why -- whether it was by order or ex officio, it makes the slightest difference. These SJB chiefs, these MUP chiefs were participating in the Crisis Staff for the reason that the Bosnian Serb leadership saw the Crisis Staffs as the best means of achieving their ends by their co-ordinating factor between the military, political which had the goals, the police and the military who carried them out. Your Honour, the ARK Crisis Staff, as we say, operated between 6th of May and the 17th July. That was the vital period for the actions that took place within the Autonomous Region of Krajina. Contrary to what is asserted in paragraph 114 of the Zupljanin brief, the Assembly of the autonomous region did not meet between April and July of 1992. It met on the 17th of July, when it verified most, if not all, of the ARK Crisis Staff decisions, and that's P1827. Moreover, whether called the Crisis Staff, or the war staff or the War Presidency, the composition remained the same, and everybody called it the Crisis Staff including the people on it. Your Honours saw briefly a part of the clip of the video P204. Can we just look at the earlier part where we see the interviews, please, of three of the major players in the Kotor Varos action.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we pause for a moment. Sorry. Your Honours, can I just pause there to note that certainly Lieutenant-Colonel Peulic, who is being interviewed there, is distinguishing between the units of the MUP and the units of the army. Yes. Next clip, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, there we see the three components together: The army, the political, and the police in the Autonomous Region of Krajina acting together, on the ground, to take over Kotor Varos and rid themselves of those who did not wish to accept Serb control. Your Honours, the importance of Zupljanin's presence on the ARK Crisis Staff can be seen from some of the matters that were discussed in the meetings. Could we have up, please, P441. First of all, we see the decision on the formation of the Crisis Staff. The war staff as printed -- the -- shall be and we see Zupljanin. The other members were, of course, Talic, Stevandic, and other persons whom Your Honours have heard about. Then can we go, please, to the next decision. This is the -- of -- we haven't got the date up, have we. I think it's April of... just a moment. No, it must be the beginning of May. I'm sorry, Your Honours, we should have put the date onto this. I've got it here. It's -- the first document was the 5th of May, and this one is -- yes, it's the 11th of May, Your Honour, I'm sorry. The deadline of the surrender of weapons who will be dealing with the -- what happens after the deadline. The weapons will be confiscated by employees of the Security Services Centre. Obviously important that the chief of the Security Services Centre was there to discuss with the other members of the Crisis Staff whether that was possible and whether they should be doing it. Then, next, Your Honour, can we look at the 13th of May. On the 16th of the May a delegation consisting of Kupresanin; Erceg; Brdjanin; Radic; Sajic, who was the national defence secretariat; Zupljanin; and others to hold talks in Knin with representatives of the RSK in establishing links in information and the economy. And then: "The security services in Banja Luka is to fully implement the decisions of the Crisis Staff on the disarming ..." Can we look, please, at the next clip. This is the 18th of May. A delegation. Again, Kupresanin, Erceg, Sajic, and Zupljanin to go to Pale and hold talks on defining the territory towards Semberija. I think that's all that I need. Thank you. Your Honours, Zupljanin himself was fully aware of the importance of the ARK Crisis Staff as the co-ordinating body for the establishment of the Serb state. Can we have a brief look, please, at P367. And, Your Honours, this is the meeting that took place on the 6th of May. In fact, it wasn't -- the report or the document recording it not produced until the 20th of May. And it contains a number of themes which we say are important when you consider Zupljanin's authority. "All my orders conveyed orally, as well those I may forward by dispatch, must be carried out. They are your law." And then goes on about the chain of command. "In all our activities, we are obliged to observe all measures and apply all procedures ordered by the Crisis Staff of the autonomous region." And then disarmament: "We ... take no action until the Crisis Staff makes the relevant decisions. It is ... important that we solve the problem comprehensively." Your Honour, again, we see over and over again in the documents produced at the time that, as far as was possible, there was to be a comprehensive and collaborative solution to the problems. And finally this, Your Honour, which goes onto deal with the next topic that I want to cover: "The chief of the CSB informed the members of the ... council that he ..." not the army, "he had established a special counter-sabotage and counter-terrorist police unit of about 150 ... The unit is made up of both active and reserve police and persons who fought on ... Slavonia battle-fronts. The unit is equipped with the most up-to-date combat equipment. Its founding will be celebrated in Banja Luka at a special ceremony marking security forces day on Tuesday, 12 May." Your Honour, for some reason, this has become of some importance in respect of Mr. Stanisic because, to be fair, there's been some confusion about it, largely because of the Glas article on the parade, which was dated the 14th, seemed to refer back to the 13th. But every other document in this case, including the video of the parade, shows that it took place on the 12th in the late afternoon after the Serb Assembly this concluded. Stanisic in his final brief asserts that it took place on the 13th and that he drove there and back again. Your Honours, however, there we have, in one short document, all these themes, as it were. And, Your Honours, we say, and we've set it out again in our brief, that the decisions made by the ARK Crisis Staff, in particular those relating to disarmament and dismissals, were forwarded by Zupljanin for action to his subordinate SJBs. Your Honours, may I then move to the special police and/or the SOS. Your Honours, the evidence of Zupljanin's participation in the formation of forces used to implement the common plan, his command and his control of those forces, the crimes committed by those forces, is fully set out in our final brief. We say it is the strongest possible evidence, and the Defence attempts to negate it through the final brief - this is the Zupljanin final brief - through selective, we say, quotation, and omission demonstrates just how powerful it is. At paragraph 172 of the Zupljanin final brief starts in its recital of facts on the special police with the ARK decision of the 27th of April. It utterly omits Zupljanin's announcement of the formation of the special police on the 15th of April. That was an announcement made to Glas newspaper, and it's P542. It is asserted in the brief that the SOS was brought into to the special police against Zupljanin's wishes and completely as a result of negotiations between the army and the SOS. Could we have up for a moment, please, P552. This, again, is an article of an interview -- an article in Glas containing an interview with Zupljanin, and he states: "As to ... SOS, which were placed upped the jurisdiction of the Security Services Centre by the ... Assembly decision, Zupljanin said ... a large number of these units' members, being reliable and experienced fighters, would be tested for engagement in the special detachment, while others would be assigned to the reserve police and the Krajina TO. The SOS would thus virtually cease to exist." And P560, please. This is Glas interviewing Zupljanin on the 12th of May and actually asking him a question about the special detachment. And what he has said -- sorry. What he says is this, that: This will be an elite unit," middle of the -- "... equipped with combat vehicles, helicopters and other contemporary equipment and weaponry." And so on and so forth. "If it is necessary for the detachment to fight together with the army, it will be made available." Now, it virtually beggars belief how it can be asserted in the light of all the evidence that this was an army unit that had no connection with or was under the control of Zupljanin and, indeed, that was resubordinated. Then he talks again about the parade on Tuesday. Or --and then he said: "This is the first time that Security --" Can we have the -- I think it's the -- that's it. Oh, well. Your Honours can see the whole article, in any event; P560. Now, Your Honours, the crimes -- actually, just a couple of the intercepts. Yes, sorry. I'm skipping something. Sorry. Your Honours, the identification, the IDs of the special police, were signed by Zupljanin. That's in 2D72 at page 9. Your Honours, at paragraph 174 of the final brief for the -- for Zupljanin, it is said that -- and for most of what is said, they rely on the evidence of Witness SZ-02. I can't remember whether he was in closed session or not so I'll just stick to it. That although they may have formally appeared to be police officers because they were issued IDs by CSB Banja Luka, in essence, they were a military unit. Again, Your Honour, at the time, Your Honours may have thought, the -- the -- the logic behind this is not apparent, why the IDs should have been signed for by Zupljanin for a unit that had nothing whatsoever to do with him. In paragraph 79, when dealing with why Zupljanin made the request for the military to provide the arms that he talks about and the equipment, it is said this was merely for logical -- sorry. "... logistical expedience as the structures were in place at the CSB as a regional centre to facilitate the delivery of such equipment." Now, leaving aside that there is not one iota of evidence that was why the request was made, how was it logistically more expedient for the army to take its equipment from its own headquarters in Banja Luka and transport them over to the CSB for a unit that was going to be a military unit? As I say, it defeats all logical thought. Your Honours, the 12th of May parade. Your Honours, we say, it's absolutely clear from the evidence you've already seen that it took place on the 12th of May. And, Your Honours, there's one other piece of evidence which deals with that which we'd like Your Honours to this time listen to. It's an intercept. It's P1124. And it is dealt with in the brief for Zupljanin as follows. We say this intercept again goes to a number of different themes. The -- paragraph 61 says: "The Prosecution's probable reliance on Zupljanin's intercepted conversation with Cedo Kljajic on the 7th of May to try and depict Zupljanin's character as anti-Muslim is far from the mark." This is when they're asserting that some of his best friends were non-Serbs. "It is clear from the conversation that they ..." that is, Kljajic and Zupljanin "... enjoyed a personal friendship, and this is reflected in the jovial and sarcastic comments recorded. The jokes in that conversation were, no doubt, in poor taste, but they were made in jest and were undoubtedly a response to the unique strains both individuals were labouring under at the time." Leaving aside there's no evidence of what strain, if any, either of these two men were labouring under, we think that Your Honours might like to hear some of the conversation as they spoke it. It's fair to say the microphone was obviously in Kljajic's office and Zupljanin is fainter. And that, may I say, Your Honours, on -- what you see on the screen is a still from the parade which we'll look at it. Zupljanin in front; Kljuc behind.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Next.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, looking at the conversation, you may think that the humour of what they were discussing is not apparent. Would Your Honours forgive me just one moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, we invite Your Honours to read through the whole transcript because there we see, we've only -- because it takes a little longer to play it, there is conversation about what should be done in Sarajevo, with Zupljanin indicating what he thinks ought to be done, and that's at pages 4 and 5 of the intercept. And, at the end, there's a conversation about the Banja Luka parade. This is the 7th of May. Cedo Kljajic is invited by Zupljanin and the minister, and the question is whether the minister can fly, and there's a discussion about helicopters. And there's also a long discussion with Serbian members of the MUP, of the new MUP, who are not doing what they ought to be doing. Can we now look, please, at the -- some of the video from the parade, which is P1393. Your Honours will see on the screen it's clearly the 12th of May, and the part of the speeches that were made.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You may have missed that. There's the date that comes up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Pause. We will see identification later. We haven't -- we have identified some of the other participants, but that is behind Zupljanin, Cedo Kljajic appearing and disappearing, with the moustache.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We do see the 12th there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is the end of the Bosnian Serb Assembly. We see Zupljanin saying this speech. While we're waiting for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is going to be identification of the various people in a minute.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, well, I say that. The version I saw stopped the film at various points, and you saw the various participants identified. Maybe it's this part.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I think -- can we just ... we'll have to re-play this clip.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go back to -- I'm sorry I'm taking the time, but I think we need to do this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, there had to be one moment when techniques went wrong. Your Honours, can I -- we'll come back to that once Mr. van Hooydonk has found the right bit. Your Honours, as far as the special police are concerned, we say that the crimes committed by the special police were well documented, particularly in Kotor Varos. Your Honours, in paragraphs 193 to 5, the Defence - the Zupljanin final brief - as I say, heavily criticise Mr. Brown for what Your Honours may recall was a misunderstanding between a document that was issued by the 1st Krajina Corps at the beginning of July, which Mr. Brown, admittedly helped along unfortunately by me, assumed related back to the killings outside the health centre in June. And he is heavily criticised. It's described somewhat slangily in paragraph 193 as scuppered by the -- by the Prosecution expert Brown. And, Your Honours, it is suggested that Brown agreed that there had not been a killing outside the health centre. That -- if Your Honours read the relevant evidence of Mr. Brown, you will see that is -- couldn't be further from the case. He accepted that he had misread the 1st Krajina Corps document, which related, apparently, as it says, to the killings of some special police, which took place later, quite clearly. But the killings outside the health centre, contrary to the Defence assertion - I'm not altogether clear whether they actually mean it - did take place and, indeed, the witness who survived the killings, who saw them, was never cross-examined on the basis that those killings did not take place. Your Honours, as far as the remainder of the evidence is concerned which shows Zupljanin's control over the special police, he ordered their release from custody. All that's said in the pre-trial brief is he didn't order that they weren't to be prosecuted. Well, Your Honours can deal with that one, I'm sure. He did all that he could in August to prevent them being disbanded. And, Your Honours, finally, we say, the Defence undermines its whole argument on this whole matter, because in paragraphs 200 and 201, they say this. And this is the first sentence: "The Defence maintains that when Zupljanin was made aware of accusations against the special police he (notwithstanding his lack of authority over the unit) refused to allow such allegations to go unaddressed." In other words, he went -- says the Defence, this wasn't a unit over which he had any control. It was a military unit, but given, however arduous his task, were controlling those who were under his commend, he went out of his way to try and address their crimes. And we say that, in itself, undermines everything. Now I don't know if we are in a position to play -- yes, Your Honours, we are. If we could just look ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I think -- although there was more, I think that will suffice. Your Honours, we say there was the classic bringing together again of all the components to the joint criminal enterprise. Your Honour, the reality, we say, is this. One uses the modern word, "a reality check." Zupljanin, the evidence shows, conformed and controlled the special police, the CSB Banja Luka special police. It was his own personal contribution, additional to the RS MUP members he already controlled through his position to the forces which implemented the take-overs. Your Honours, that the police took part in the take-overs, as you've heard, is clear, from the witness testimony and from the reports prepared by the MUP themselves. Your Honour, finally, can I deal with the question of detention facilities and Zupljanin, because we cover this aspect very fully in the final brief. But the assertions are made in the Zupljanin final brief that all detention facilities were the responsibility of the army as the MUP was not allowed to guard them. I've already dealt with the missing logical progression in that. That Zupljanin was unaware of their existence until shortly before July the 11th meeting. That's paragraph 299. And that he took an initiative to form a commission and accordingly was instrumental in the closure of Omarska and Keraterm. That is paragraphs 286 and 312. Your Honours, in the light of that, it's necessary, very shortly, to rehearse some of the evidence. We say that that evidence shows that the incarceration of the non-Serbs in these camps and the subsequent removal from the area was a primary method of achieving the objective of the Bosnian Serb plan. Of the 22 detention facilities, as Mr. Demirdjian has already shown you, that were listed -- are listed in the indictment, only one of them was under the jurisdiction of the VRS, but it was the police, as Your Honours know, who brought the majority of the prisoners to Manjaca, Kljuc, and Sanski Most in particular. They took part in the interrogations and the classifications in Manjaca. So they or -- and guarded some of the facilities. So although it was a military camp run by Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic, the police, too, had an input into that. Your Honour, when Omarska was established in May, Drljaca sent a copy of his order about Omarska to the CSB in Banja Luka. That is P1560. So it is really not possible for Zupljanin to say that he was unaware of the establishment of these camps. On 13th of June, Drljaca wrote to Zupljanin complaining about the treatment being meted out by the special police. Your Honours, that's P659. Your Honour, it is very interesting that Drljaca, who is supposed to be this rogue, this person over Zupljanin, had no control, virtually is one of the more assiduous reporters of matters to Zupljanin of any of the SJB chiefs. By June, Radulovic was warning his superiors in the SNB that the International Committee of the Red Cross was really exhibiting increasing interest in visiting the collection centres. That's P1391. So, again, that's before he actually spoke to Zupljanin about it. And in June, the same month, Muslim representatives held a meeting with General Talic about what was going on in Banja Luka. The persecutions and the delegation facilities. That's P459.19. And there they complain to General Talic. And General Talic, at the end of that meeting, if we can perhaps go to the next slide -- no, sorry. I thought it was on there. But, in fact, he tells them he will write to Zupljanin about the other collection centres over which the army has no control. Your Honours, at the July 11 meeting, it is said in the -- in the -- in the brief, that, "as a result of his submissions at that meeting, conditions improved and Prijedor was eventually closed down." If one looks, please, very briefly at page 7 his actual intent is that the army and Crisis Staffs or War Presidencies are requesting that as many Muslims as possible are gathered, and they are leaving these undefined camps up to the internal affairs organs. And he goes on to say -- at no stage does he say, This is all the army, and we should insist that these camps are closed down. Your Honour, from the moment, in fact, that the camps became known to the international community, the MUP tried to shift responsibility to the army, and you will see that in P1818. Now, Your Honours, not once in the final brief is there any mention that, in fact, as everybody knows, the reason that these camps were closed down was the visit by international reporters, and to assert, as Zupljanin asserts, that it was his action at the 11th of July which was responsible and, indeed, his subsequent commission, Your Honours, is, again, we say, without any foundation at all. Indeed, by the time the internationals got there on the 6th of August, Keraterm had already been closed, and most of the Omarska prisoners, as we saw in that clip, had been moved to Trnopolje. Before that happened, Zupljanin had visited Omarska had no less than two occasions. And, Your Honour, the report, the commission report which covers only three out of the municipalities [sic] under his control, which, on his order, had to be completed in three days, Your Honours may think was nothing more than a whitewash. That report being P602. Your Honours, obviously, we've had to allocate the time, and I've reached the end of what we say about Zupljanin. The Defence rely -- when I say what we say about Zupljanin, obviously we have had a great deal more to say in what we wrote. The Defence rely very heavily on the document that he sent on the 30th of July where he was apparently saying that the police should not be taking orders from Crisis Staffs and the like. Your Honours will look at the document. It's 2D25. And you may think that if the reason for sending it is possibly quite clear, that there were a lot of complaints coming about -- from the Serbs themselves about the behaviour of the police, and it was a document, we suggest when you read the whole thing, is no more than, as it were, shifting responsibility. There's no clear instruction given. There's no resume of what it is in -- in detail that they are complaining about. And the one document perhaps that we should look at is one that he sent on the 20th of July to the MUP headquarters, which, needless to say, I don't think I have made a note of. But, Your Honours, it's -- no, I haven't -- I'll have to come back to that and I'll mention that tomorrow. Your Honours, finally on the question of intent, the Defence say that Zupljanin was never heard to say anything discriminatory against non-Serbs. In fact, the theme that comes out very strongly from a number of witnesses who spoke to Zupljanin and complained to him about what was happening was effectively there was nothing he could do. Well, Your Honours, he wasn't a Brdjanin, he wasn't a Vukic, he wasn't a Kalinic. He didn't use words in the way that they did to drive out those who were terrified. But we say if you look at his actions, they have no other explanation but of his whole-hearted endorsement of, and mixing with, involvement in, the Bosnian Serb plan. Your Honours, we've got five minutes, but whether it is worth Mr. Hannis starting, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... Before we take the adjournment for the day, with regard to the Prosecution's request seeking leave to file a written motion to address what it argues are errors of law in the Defence trial briefs, the Trial Chamber notes that the Prosecution has had an opportunity to make its submissions on the law in its final trial brief. Moreover, the Chamber has granted the parties an additional hour for their closing arguments, in order to give the parties more time to attend to what was raised in the final trial briefs. For these reasons, the Chamber denies the Prosecution's request. So we take the adjournment until 9.00 tomorrow morning.
